utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Who's going to take the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls Mr. Normand Boucher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Ms. Gustafson, is the witness a native English or French-speaking person?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Native French-speaking, Your Honour, but he will be testifying in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Boucher. Before you give evidence in this Court, the rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The next will now be handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boucher. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Boucher, from what I understand, you speak French and English. If you have problems whilst you speak English, you can and you may speak French. We do have French-speaking interpreters, and there is absolutely no problem. But I have understood that you have chosen to speak in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I -- my mother tongue is French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [No interpretation] -- in English, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Boucher.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Normand Boucher.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And could the witness please be shown 65 ter number 6540.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher, do you recognise the statement on the screen as a type written version of a handwritten statement that you gave and signed on the 11th of February, 1996?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And could the witness please be shown 65 ter number 6451?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, just on the transcript the previous 65 ter number was 6540, whereas on my list I have 6450, instead of 6540.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I misspoke, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then the statement of 1996 is 6450. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Boucher, do you recognise this statement as one that you gave on the 11th and 12th of November, 1999?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally could the witness please be shown 65 ter number 6542. And, Mr. Boucher, do you recognise this statement as one that you began to give in April of 2008, finished on the 5th of November, 2008, and signed on the 24th of November, 2008.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I do recall this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And taken together, are these three statements true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And do they accurately reflect what you said at the time that they were taken?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if I asked you today in court the same questions you were asked when you gave those statements, would you give the Court the same answers?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender those three statements into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, and from the Gotovina Defence a message was received, there's no objection against any --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar, would you please assign numbers to the statements.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, 65 ter number 6450 becomes exhibit number P1176. 65 ter number 6451 becomes exhibit number P1177. And 65 ter number 6452 becomes exhibit number P1178.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. P1176, P1177, and P1178 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if I could provide the witness with hard copies of those statements, and if I could read a summary of his statements into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have explained to Mr. Boucher what the purpose of that is?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Normand Boucher was a UNCIVPOL officer stationed in Knin from March 1995 until approximately 22nd August 1995. On the morning of the 4th of August, 1995, he was awakened by the sound of a shell hitting a nearby house at 5.00 a.m. As he was making his way to the basement, a shell hit his house. He took refuge in the basement of his house, where he stayed for approximately two hours. He then moved to the basement of a nearby house. A few hours later, he made his way to the downtown area where he took refuge in a tall building. Along the way, he saw shelling damage. Mr. Boucher was picked up by a UN APC at approximately 7.00 p.m. on the 4th of August, 1995, and was taken to the UN compound. Mr. Boucher was permitted to leave the UN compound to conduct a foot patrol of Knin around 7 August 1995 with another UNCIVPOL monitor. In Knin, Mr. Boucher saw soldiers coming out of houses carrying clothes and household items, and he saw soldiers loading electronic items into a truck marked Puma Brigade. Around the 11th of August, Mr. Boucher witnessed an incident of burning houses and crops involving soldiers with a Puma Brigade truck in Kosovo village. In Mr. Boucher's assessment, the Croatian civilian police did nothing to stop the burning and killing in the area after Operation Storm and were unable to stop military personnel from committing crimes. And that concludes the summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, the statement starts that I was in Sector South from March 1995 when, in fact, I started in January 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I was referring to your time based in Knin, but in any event, the summary is not part of the record, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing at the imprecision, Mr. Boucher. I think Ms. Gustafson explained now that she was actually referring to Knin, rather than to Sector South. But your statement is in evidence. This is just to inform the public about what is in your statement. But nevertheless, they should be rightly informed. I agree with that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown 65 ter number 6497. This is a marked photograph of Knin, and I have hard copies to distribute so it is easier for the witness and the parties and the Bench to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of what expect to be the nature of this document, may I take it that there is no objection against adding it to the 65 ter list because it does not appear on the list yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is true for all Defence teams, so it is added now to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher, do you recognise this photograph as one that you marked yesterday and which you identified a number of locations that you mentioned in your statements?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I do recognise this, and I would like to point out that I did have a chance to speak with the Defence who provided a larger map, and some of the indication, for example, of the house I was living in was clearer on the larger map than this one. It's a very close neighbourhood, but it's a matter of maybe a street over. And also the house where I moved to for my second protection, and also the house -- one of the house next door, for example, that two CIVPOL monitors lived, was maybe more correct on the bigger map, but the rest of it is the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Is there anything you would like to correct that you realize now is incorrect on this photograph you have before you?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Like I say, just the identification of my residence that I was renting, which is A. C is the location of the Knin CIVPOL -- sorry, not the CIVPOL office. It's the --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could take them one by one, the locations that you would like to correct.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If the exhibit could be brought up on the screen, and if there's corrections, they could be made electronically.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Location A you marked as your house. Is that correct, or would you like to correct the location you marked as your house, as A?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I would put it a little bit further -- would you look on the picture now a little bit further more, to the top. So it is probably one street further or higher up.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Perhaps if the witness could be given a red marker, and he could mark with an X the location of his house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then we have to -- it doesn't make sense to add more to what we see at this moment. Then I suggest that -- because we can't remove anything from this marked map because the markings are not electronically made. So therefore, we would have to zoom in, and I must say that where the line connecting A to one of the two small circles which appear to create an 8 within a wider circle, it's not entirely clear whether the A goes to the lower or to the upper part of what I now call an 8. So therefore, perhaps if we have either a clean map or another map, the witness said that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Frankly, if I can be of some assistance, the only thing that we didn't discuss with Mr. Boucher yesterday was, Take P62 and go to that area and blow that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was no more mysterious than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, no one complained about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, no, I'm saying that was able to see his house more clearly. I think that it is difficult on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would then suggest that we invite the witness to mark with more precision on P62 - is that the clean map? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and then blow it up and then to have more details about perhaps, A, D, and K, which are very close to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If the witness could be shown P62, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Loading maps takes a while, Mr. Boucher. Could we zoom in on the -- a little bit below left of the centre of this picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we go to the left of where it says Knin general supply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There we are. Could we invite the witness with the colour for Prosecution is ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I believe it's red, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's red.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I will put a circle around where my house was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you mark that with an A.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The location of the house where the CIVPOL monitors lived that was partly destroyed is D. It's right there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I don't think that there is any need to mark again the -- the residential area. That appears to be clear on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Are those the only two locations that you needed to correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: The only other thing is when I moved to the tall building on the map you had shown me, again being a bit smaller, it was a bit confusing. But with the larger scale as it is now, I have a better chance to show you exactly where this house or this building is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Are you able to locate that on this map now? Could you mark that with an F.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in the other map, you also marked the neighbouring building where you later saw damage. Can you mark that on this as well, as G.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Is that everything then, the corrections that you needed to make?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the original map and this correction could be given one exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can they be joined?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's not a problem. They will become exhibit number P1179.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that just as there's no objection against adding it to the 65 ter list that there is no objection against admission into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is then true for the map with markings A up to and including M and the more precise markings of A, B, F, and G, on a second map marked electronically. Mr. Registrar, that 1179 is admitted into evidence. I should say P1179.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Boucher, just staying with that map for a moment, the location -- the large circle that you marked K, where it was -- you labelled it as a residential area where you saw a lot of damaged houses, are you able to estimate for the Court how many houses you saw damaged in that area you marked as K?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It would have to be a guesstimate, but I would think they would be something in the neighbourhood of about eight to ten.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the extent of the damage to the house that you lived in?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It looked like a shell -- I must clarify one thing as I start. I have no military experience. And when you talk about the different kinds of fire-power that military has, I have no clue. I'm a police officer, so with smaller weapons. So the damage that occurred to my residence that I was renting was a shell that was fired from far away, went through the roof and into the house, the attic, and into the apartment. I was renting the upstairs apartment of this house.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And how much damage to the structure did the shell cause?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, houses are made of cement, so it takes a lot of rounds to really destroy a house. The roofs and the red clay, of course, they break fairly easy. The cement which is actually the floor of the attic is also in cement, and all of it is with -- is rebarred, in other words there is metal in there to make sure that the cement doesn't break away. And as the residence explained to me, houses are made that way to prevent them from crumbling in an earthquake situation. So the shell went through the roof, of course, blew away a large hole of the red clay tiles, broke some of the wood that supports it, and made a hole through the floor of the attic and into the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. The same question with respect to the house where the CIVPOL monitors lived, the one you marked as D. What was the extent of the damage to that structure?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That house received -- I would call it shelling, again, large projectiles on the side of the house which created a big crater, a big hole, on the side of the house. The hole would have been, I suspect, about a metre big, diameter.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And the building you marked as G, the one next to the one you took shelter in, the taller building in the downtown area, do you know what the use of that building was prior to Operation Storm? Was it residential, commercial?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Both building F, where I took refuge to protect myself, and G were both residential apartment buildings, and I would think they were about six storeys high, five or six storeys high.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like that ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, would you allow me two questions to clarify some of the answers. And perhaps first, I should start with a further explanation of the markings, because at a later moment, people might have some difficulties in exactly understanding the markings. The markings are two small circles, the one just above the other, above the two of them. Letter A which relates to the upper circle. To the right of the lower circle, we find, although a bit unclear, a D, which refers to the lower small circle. So D should not be confused as a location, but just a marking to the right of the lower circle. Then I'd like to ask one question: You talked about a hole in the wall of -- of the house where the CIVPOL monitors lived. Now a hole, did it go all through the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you could look through it into the interior of the house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In your 2008 statement at paragraph 15, you described what you saw that day on the 4th of August in the streets. You said: "From what I saw on the streets that day, people were running everywhere and vehicles were stalling because of lack of fuel. It was mayhem." And I'd just like to ask you, were you able to gather from the people that you saw on the streets and in the buildings that day what their psychological or emotional state was?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, I did. Not when people were running everywhere, but I did very soon after, and that's starting from the point which was about 10.00 in the morning when I took refuge in building F. The residents that were in the basement, there were a lot of resident there is, of course, crying and talking because some people came from other areas to protect themselves in that large building. There were some comments there. I could understand some of the conversation. There were some people in that basement also that spoke English, and clearly identified their frantic situation. And from that point, also after 7.00 at night when I arrived at the UN camp, there were people who were actually interpreters, of course, their English being much better, would have -- would explain what happened during the time they were trying to find their way to the UN camp, and also would relate comments from other residents. But even before this, there are important events that took place that had people on edge for quite a few days before this. Do you want me to cover this?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think that's covered in your statement. I just wanted to get a sense of the actual situation on the 4th. And you said that people were running everywhere and vehicles were stalling. Were you able to gather from your travels on the streets where people were attempting to go?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, in my statement I covered that I tried to get a direction. I had asked the chief of the milicija, the Serb police, before the attack if there was a plan, and he didn't even want to talk about this, discarding it as if we don't need it. So from this, I gathered there was no plan, and people were left on their own, I guess, to fend. The one thing you have to remember is that sector, like all four sectors, there was really very little articles and fuel and whatever else that came in, in the sectors, except for a lot of black market, including some of our UN vehicles were getting siphon of fuel and whatever. The other things is if there is no plan -- and people, where are they going is my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could just stop you. That was my question. Were you able to get a sense, based on your observations on the 4th, where people were going or not? If you didn't, that's fine too.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I had no idea. I know there were people that knew some dirt roads that led out of the sector through Bosnia. I had heard about this many times from different -- you know, observations from other groups and from some interpreters and citizens, but I did not know where these roads were, and I didn't think that a lot of residents had reliable vehicle, for example, to make it. Like, a lot of Ladas, they only work when they felt like it, and so on. So not very reliable modes of getting out of there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You're talking about modes of getting out of there. Did it appear that people were attempting to leave Knin on that day?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It actually started before that day. Again, going back to --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Boucher. I'm going interrupt you. That is in your statement as well. But based on what you could see on the 4th, did it appear that people, on the 4th, were attempting to leave Knin?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to move to another topic which is the foot patrol that you described, and that's at paragraphs 55 to 56 of your 1999 statement, as well paragraphs 21 to 26 of your 2008 statement. This is a foot patrol that you described conducting with the Swedish CIVPOL monitor on about the 7th of August. At paragraph 55 of your 1999 statement you said: "Everywhere I looked I saw soldiers coming out of houses, carrying with them everything which a house would contain, clothes, household goods, et cetera. The soldiers were laughing as they did this." And I'd like to ask you, are you able to estimate for the Court how many soldiers you saw during that patrol carrying goods out of houses like this?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: 13 and a half years later, my memory misses it a bit. But in 1999 if I said that statement, I would hold by it. The number of people or soldiers that would be actually doing this, I can't recall, but I know there was, and several of them. Exact numbers, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And from what you recall, were the soldiers during this more or less openly, or were they trying to hide what they were doing, or could you tell?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It was very open.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And was there any reaction by the soldiers to the presence of you and your colleague?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes. There was a comments, yelling, whistling, and so on. And actually there was a lot of soldiers that were already drunk, out of control, I would think, or certainly not professional. So, yeah, they were -- and, again, I estimate them to be -- I never saw one where I could identify there was ranks on their shoulder or on their arms, so they were obviously of the private category, I suppose, or the enter-level soldiers so -- and, again, what number -- there was some in different parts where we walk right from outside of the UN camp going all the way to the bridge, and then into the downtown there was some, and they were moving about. I could not see -- there was no confrontation at this point that I could see, otherwise we probably would not have been there. And then going in to where my house was, very close on one of those streets, there was actually even a truck, and they were loading, you know, TVs and VCRs and electronics and whatever else.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And during that patrol, did you see any civilians or only soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing civilians per se. I don't recall. That's not clear in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And were the soldiers in uniform?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, all of them were in uniform, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And can you -- are you able now to describe the uniform?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, they're camouflage-type uniform, combat uniform. Not dress if want, what you would show in a parade, but really confrontation-type uniforms. Camouflage, I guess, I would call it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you said that they were shooting in the area. Do you recall the kind of weapons that they had? Were they -- what kind of weapons they had?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, most of them had access to -- they would probably be AK-47 was the type of weapons that they had. I don't recall pistols, for example. Pistols, to me, would have identified probably officer or a little bit higher ranks, but I didn't see any of those. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry. These were automatic weapons?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you talked a moment ago about seeing soldiers loading TVs and VCRs into a truck, and you've described this in your statement. And in your statement you said it was a truck marked "Puma Brigade." And you also described the Puma Brigade sign. You said it had a black Puma on it with the name Puma. I'd like to show you a picture --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown P281.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I note from my conversations with Mr. Boucher yesterday that he was shown the one photograph of the Puma badges, as opposed to a spread or a multitude and, of course, showing one, and being the one that is on the screen. So certainly I note the methodology that was employed by the Prosecution which we have objected to previously, and I do believe that -- Your Honour, and I don't have the transcript, did express some caution about that methodology.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The witness did -- was asked to describe the badge in the statements before it was shown to him, and I believe that the objection previously was about a photo spread of individuals, not -- I don't recall this coming up with --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, much depends on -- I think an identification procedure should always start with asking a witness to describe something. Then sometimes a description is such that could you not find more species which meet the description. For example, if I say the person had a sun tattooed on his right cheek, then it might be very difficult to find six persons with tattoos on the right cheek showing the sun. Now, here apparently, the witness in his statement described names, whatever happens now in court, if this has been done before the witness entered court, we all know that an identification as such in court is -- doesn't add anything to the identification done outside of court, so the only reasonable question to put to him is, Is this the emblem or are these the insignia you identified earlier? And then what to do with that, is still to be seen. But it makes no sense, the first identification. And when I refer to identification, of course, usually it's faces, persons, but the first one is decisive to the extent that whatever happens later, it's not a fresh identification, where a choice has been given. So let's move on. The -- if there is -- if a number of similar emblems do exist, then it would have been preferable to put more emblems to the witness even out of court, and told that he can identify that he can make a selection among them. But this apparently has not happened. This is now on the record. At the same time, of course, he has described a specific name to it. We'll see. Mr. Kehoe, I think that this properly identifies the problem you raise, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's now on the record. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just to clarify this identification happened yesterday, and I simply wanted to put that on the record. And in terms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If would you have -- again, I do not know what the choice would have been, whether it would have been possible or not possible to compose a sheet. I don't know whether there are more.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Not based on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will tell that you the Prosecutor provided us with a series of badges as part of their tests list.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's true, Your Honour. This badge and no other similar badges appear in that book. There's nothing that could have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any other badge with the name Puma on it?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I haven't looked at it recently, Your Honour, but I believe not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is the case, then we are more or less in the area with the man with the sun tattooed on his right cheek.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, there is a multitude of badges, and we had a situation about previous witnesses who testified, and I can give you name of the individual who testify, about the unit that was there and convinced that it was there, and identified the badge. And that unit was somehow well north -- to the north in Sector North and not in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're raising another matter than I was addressing at this moment. That is whether a photo spread of various, all bearing the name Puma could be created, yes or not. Because that, to some extent, could explain or could be the floor of what was presented to the witness yesterday. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher, were you shown this badge yesterday?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did you yesterday recognise it as the badge, or the sign that you saw?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I also mentioned that some vehicles actually had the letters "Puma" on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Not necessarily with this badge all the time, but just the word "Puma" on the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So to clarify, you sometimes saw this sign and sometimes just the word "Puma?"

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And the truck that you saw on the patrol that you took, where on the truck was the sign?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I can't positively say anymore. It was on the vehicle. Otherwise, I wouldn't have recorded it in my head. But was it on the door or on the fender or on the front hood of the truck? I'm not sure at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And at paragraph 26 of your 2008 statement, you said you didn't recall passing any check-points during this patrol. I'd like to ask you more generally, in the days following Operation Storm, do you recall seeing any check-points that had been set up by the Croatian police or the military?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: The only check-point or place where we were actually stopped to go was at the -- the cemetery. I do not recall any check-points in any other place, and so in my mind, we had pretty free access -- that was the first day on foot only, although they were yelling at us and whatever and whistling and screaming names. We were not -- in my mind, we were not checked, stopped, to say, Where are you going and so on, and there was no place where you had to show them UN identification or anything like that. So I don't recall any check-point. Of course, we were limited. And that day, on foot, we did not reach the cemetery, so there was -- that was later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move to another topic, which is the next patrol that you described taking, around the 8th of August, when you discovered several dead bodies. And the first one I'd like to ask you about is -- this is at paragraph 58 of your 1999 statement. You described finding the corpse of a man in uniform on a hilltop on the road to Drnis who had been shot through the head. And I would just like to ask you, how did you discover this body?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: You have to remember, this is August, it is very hot. Smell of any dead people or animals and so on. But this one here was right by the side of the road. And in my identification and my statement, I said it was on the road to Drnis. But, in fact, when you leave Knin and go up the hill, there is several curves on the way to Drnis, but right on top of the hill, you can turn right - and I forget the name of this small village. You can turn right, and it was on the top of the hill. So it is not really the road, complete road, or the clear road, to Drnis but another side road, and there was a body right on the side of the road. First of all, the smell, you would have the smell, and then, secondly, because it is summer, the body is all swollen up. It becomes about double the size that normally it would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you saw this body?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you said it had been shot through the head. Did you see the wound?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And how close were you able to inspect the wound?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, without gloves, you really don't wanted to touch bodies, in the summer, particularly. But within few feet, two feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: As a police officer, did you have some experience with bullet wounds, identifying bullet wounds?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, again, this is summer. It's dated, within a matter of a day, for example, the body will decompose a lot faster than in the winter when it freezes and so on. But when you have a hole on the side of the head, then it becomes pretty obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Are you able, and if you're not able, then please tell the Court, to estimate the range at which the person was shot?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I cannot say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, could we ask the witness, because top of the hill, side street, whether you would be able to identify the place where you saw the body on the map, so that we have precise information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have P69 then on the screen again so that the witness could tell us what you could tell us -- what you could do is give instructions how to move the cursor so that we know where it is, and we could ask the witness then to mark it, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the map that have I seen so far would not include that road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we refrain from using that map. It's outside the scope of that map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like that ask you about the two bodies that you found, the man and the woman. And you describe this as leaving the town, up the hill, direction Gracac. And I'd like to ask you, how did you discover these two bodies?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I believe it one of the CIVPOL monitors that said there were two bodies on the road, and there was a little tractor. A lot of people would vehiculate with a tractor. They would sit in the little trailer and then, you know, control the tractor. The tractor's on the side, there's clothes all over, and there's a man and a woman, a man in uniform, a woman not in uniform, again, shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And were you able to -- in your statement you described them as being both shot in the head. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And how close were you to the bodies when you saw these wounds?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: A metre.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And where were the bodies in relation to each other? How close together were they?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Maybe two metres apart.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in relation to the tractor?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: The tractor was almost in the middle of the road, so that's why it was pretty obvious. You couldn't miss. You had to drive around it. And the body were more on the side of the road, and then, again, like I said, there was clothes around it, and -- that's it. That's the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move on to the incident you describe of the burning you witnessed in Kosovo village, and you describe this as sometime around the 11th of August. And it's described primarily at paragraph 71, 72 of your 1999 statement. If you could just is describe to the Court in your own words what you -- what you witnessed that day, please.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, I had a scheduled meeting to see the chief of the policija, that's the -- and I don't know the different ranks in chiefs that they have or had. But the chief for the Dalmatia region was in Sibenik. So you had to go through Drnis -- from Knin to Drnis and then on to Sibenik. And as you leave Knin, you go through a village that's call Kosovo. And as I drove on my way to Sibenik, this is when I saw the again small -- smaller vehicle, truck-type, green in colour, with soldiers taking out cans that what appeared to me like gas can, I suppose, jerrycan is what we call it in Canada, and they were taking them out of the back of this truck and going toward the houses. And, of course, I had a meeting to go and so on, so I kept on going. And on the way back -- the houses were not on fire then. On the way back the houses were on fire and there was part of the corn crops and so on also on fire. So my deduction was that they went there, and they were actually walking with cans going towards houses, that they were set on fire. I did not see them light it up or spread gas on the building or anything like this. But it appeared to be that was what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when you returned and saw the houses on fire, can you estimate now how many houses you saw burning or burnt?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, in that area, there's about -- I would say about eight to ten houses right by the road, and then there's quite a few that are actually fairly far from the road. In other words, there's another dirt road, I think, that goes in the back, and I think it's a dirt road. And it would have maybe in the neighbourhood of about 20 to 25 houses back there. So the houses by the roads were on fire when I came back, or at least still smoking and the roofs -- the only thing that burns is the wood that supports and then furniture inside. That's still on fire. And then can you see that the houses far away are also on fire, except for a few. Of course, there's so much smoke, it's hard to see, but I noticed later on further trips that way that there was a few houses that were not burnt.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I'd like to show you a video. This is P847, and we have it set up in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "My name is Soren Liborius. I worked for ECMM during and after Operation Storm in August 1995. Today is 18th of May 1997. We are looking in the direction of the road going from Knin down to Drnis, going south down to Drnis, and we are in the northern end of the Kosovo valley, located immediately south of the Knin valley."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may it, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we stop. I was about to stop you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do believe that there a -- this is 92 ter testimony, and it's certainly not applicable to this particular witness, and if this is 92 ter information or prior testimony, which is what it is is, that should be put to the witness, that's the procedure. Absent that, there is no -- there no methodology to allow this monologue to go on that's included in this tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had a different problem on my mind. But we'll pay attention to you. That is, that there was translation in B/C/S, but there was no translation in French. Have you provided the booth with the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I had -- mistakenly, I thought that because it was an exhibit, I didn't need to do that, but I understand that I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the completeness -- first of all, it is an exhibit, but we are playing not the whole of the exhibit. I think we started at 41.20.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I believe that's where the exhibit starts, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That could be. I don't have a recollection precise enough to know that. So that is a --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm happy to play it without the sound, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just want to show the pictures to the -- yes. As far as the objection where Mr. Kehoe was concerned, let me try to fully understand you. Of course, I do not know exactly what I can expect to see at this moment. The witness has described what he saw on his way when he passed through the village of Kosovo and upon return, what he saw. Now, I understood that Ms. Gustafson would play a video related to that. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and it's -- it's -- I'm not sure what the objection is related to 92 ter submission, but There's a video, and I'd like the witness to look at the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My objection is this, Judge: This is this video with this dialogue by Mr. Liborius is part of their 92 ter submission, so it is testimony in the case that has been offered into evidence by the Prosecution. So the procedure on this score has always been, if we're going to confront a witness with testimony of someone else, then that person, this particular witness in this case, Mr. Boucher, needs to be asked about that first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know what -- what will be shown, but I expected that what Ms. Gustafson was about to show was related to the evidence elicited just a minute ago by -- through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I have no intention of putting anyone's statement on this matter to the witness. This is video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The video has the dialogue or the monologue listed below. The video that we just saw had the writing that -- that Mr. Liborius was speaking on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Ms. Gustafson now offered to present this video without spoken words, and, of course, I do know that you still could read it. But if we would instruct the witness to focus on the picture and not to read the text below, then at least to that extent, that would meet your objection, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. President, I just ask technologically whether the screen can be shown to the witness without the particular writing underneath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that that would be easy, because it is an integral part, from what I understand, from the picture, the text, but if we would invite Mr. Boucher to -- to ignore and to refrain from reading the text below and the text not to be made audible, then we could proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. In the interests of transparency, the witness has seen the video with the audio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's good that Ms. Gustafson informs us about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's play the video again. Mr. Boucher, I would like to instruct you that you should look at the pictures and ignore any text. Just look at the pictures.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The text has been taken off, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been taken off. So therefore, I was too quick in saying that it might be difficult. We started a minute ago at 41:20, so let's start there again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher couldn't ignore this text, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could just stop there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Boucher, you were shown this video yesterday. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you recognise this road?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes. This is the road that leads to Drnis.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I can add to that the first stop was at 41:35.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could stop there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher, did you recognise that scene?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly what I tried to mention earlier. There was some houses close to the road that were burnt, and then there's several houses, maybe 25, 27, 30 houses further away, closer to the mountain or that little hill at the back which is actually serviced through a separate road, but it is all part of this Kosovo village, if you want. Some of the houses at the back were not burnt. But the ones on the road, I think all of them were burnt.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The houses that can you see now, are those the ones that you described as being close to the road?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could move the video back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second stop was made at 42:39.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could stop there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Are these houses that you saw burning?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And are these the ones that you describe the as being further away?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes. And there's also some crops of corn and different kinds of grains and gardens, if you want, broken down there small patches, if you want, and some of them were also on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And we're now at 42:41.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You described this incident as occurring on approximately the 11th of August. There is other evidence - and I'm referring in particular to P830 which is in the ECMM report - that this incident may have occurred on the 10th of August. Is it possible that you may be mistaken and, in fact, you saw this on the 10th?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: My information is not based on what I heard from ECMM or other types of services or agencies, Red Cross, UNHCR. It's the comments that -- that, in my mind, this was a day I was travelling to see the chief of policija in Sibenik, and the best of my recollection, it's the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And could the witness now be shown 65 ter 4062, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In your most recent statement you recognised this document as a protest letter that you wrote to General Cermak, in relation to your attempts to gain access to the Knin cemetery?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask you about the first line, where you say -- you refer to: "Refusals from your personnel to give UNCIVPOL access to the Orthodox cemetery near Kninsko Polje." When you talked about your personnel, who were you referring to? Who was denying you access to the cemetery at this time?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: At first it was the military. There was people on green uniforms, not allowing not allowing CIVPOL monitors to get close to the cemetery. And a little bit later, it was the policija.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: When you referred in this letter to your personnel, were you referring to the military or the police or both?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, in my mind, I think, General Cermak had been appointed as - if the translation is right - as the governor of Knin, and I thought he had authority over military and police.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could tender this document into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P1180, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1180 is admitted into evidence. I've heard of no objections. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if the witness could be shown 65 ter number 2043, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Boucher, again, in your most recent statement at paragraph 35, you describe this statement as the response you received from General Cermak to your protest letter.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, contact Mr. Romanic in relation to accessing the cemetery in accordance with this letter?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: My trip to Mr. Grgurcin, who was the chief -- Mr. Romanic's chief, if you want, his boss, in Sibenik, I discussed that with him. And there was a comment which is in my statement, that the police did not override military, and which is actually a very common - probably in most countries - once the military has an operation, the police certainly cannot stop it. And one of his comments, which is again in the statement, is the military is the military, they do what they want to.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm just wanting you to focus on this particular letter. Did you contact Mr. Romanic after receiving this letter, in relation to accessing the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But after taking about Mr. Grgurcin, he advised me, Going back to see Cedo Romanic, and he will give you a note from the policija to give you access to wherever you want to go, and I did this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in your statement you described going to the cemetery yourself after receiving permission from Romanic. And what happened when you went to the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Was not allowed access. Couldn't -- the road -- actually both ends of this little road were stopped, and you couldn't get in.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Stopped. Did somebody stop you?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes. There was somebody right at the intersection where you turn to get on to the cemetery. No cars were going through. The road was blocked. And at the other end of it, which is closer to the hospital that part, too, was also blocked.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Blocked by whom?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: The military.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The military at that point?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did you ever learn why you were being denied access to the Knin cemetery?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: No. Reality is -- and I don't know how many times I said this in meetings with officials or policija. Our role was to monitor, and the sooner we can monitor whatever is happening, the sooner we're out of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did anyone you spoke to in the police or the military give you any reason, to your recollection, why you couldn't access the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: No. A comment for a lot of areas, for example, was, For your own safety, stay out. But I don't think they used that line there. Just you're not allowed to go in.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could tender 65 ter 2043 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit PP1181.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1181 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There's just one last brief topic I would like to go over, which is your conversations with the Colonel in the Croatian army that you knew as Colonel Zelic. And you described in your most recent statement at paragraph 18 that you met him four or five times. And you also stated that you complained to Colonel Zelic about the behaviour of his soldiers, and he told you they were just celebrating. That was at paragraph 18 of your most recent statement. Do you recall now what specifically you complained about, in terms of the behaviour of the soldiers to Colonel Zelic?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: If you give me a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, all the times that I met with him, I was at the gate, and I'll just give you a little bit of brief why I was there and why he would show up. When it was code red, I was not CIVPOL anymore, I answered to the commander of the UN. And the task that he had assign the me, and my monitors, the main task was to receive refugees that were coming in, so please man the gate, take names, and so on. And whoever would show up at the gate, there was a lot of soldiers coming up on their own, breaking ranks, if you want, asking is somebody here, they are pointing guns everywhere, actually. It was -- to me, not very professional in manner, very excited, and so on. There was a lot of drinking. Could you hear them yelling and whatever else, even from the camp, which is not invest from there, several houses, drinking, and even shooting. They weren't that far. So in one of the times that -- I think he is a colonel from the translation. Colonel Zelic showed up. I said him, I said, you know, Is there any way -- first of all, I always ask can we go out, because we weren't allowed to go out for our own protection. That was the main comment. But I said you know, Could we stop this? And he said they're just having fun. They went through dishes and so on and confrontation, and now they're just celebrating.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So when you were having this conversation, was this at the time that you saw the soldiers drinking and shooting in front of the gate, so you were --

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You were referring to what was happening --

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- in front of you and Colonel Zelic?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Wasn't right at this moment, but it happened over a period of hours and -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Those are my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boucher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Gustafson, looking at your exhibit list, I see that, of course, the statements, we've dealt with them. Protest letter, response to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There's nothing else on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing else because we have 3374 and 292 and 6494, you leave them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Who will be the first to cross-examine Mr. Boucher? Mr. Kehoe, we are approximately ten minutes from where we usually would have a break. If you would prefer to start after the break, then we would have an earlier break. But if you say, No, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is preferable, Your Honour, just to get a little set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Boucher, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No. I way saying if we could take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, you could take the break now. I misunderstood you. Yes. I should have understood you well. I said if you would prefer, and you said it was preferable, so I should have better listened to you. We will have a break, and we'll resume at quarter to 11.00. But you know what will happen after the break, Mr. Boucher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Boucher.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It seems like only last night that we were together.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It was last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher, you met with the Gotovina Defence team on two occasions in January of 2008 and last night, being the 17th of December, 2008. And do you recall giving us the -- a statement last night that you signed?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think I provided you a copy --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer for the purposes of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies. If we could bring up on the screen 1D00-0750. Mr. President, I have to say that we finalized this last night with Mr. Boucher. This there is no B/C/S version at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The main interested party in having the B/C/S version is the Defence. So, therefore, without objections by other Defence teams, the Chamber will allow you to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher, if we can just look through this. This is -- you see your signature at the front or the bottom of this page?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I believe that during the course of this, you initialed every page. And if we could go to the final page of this document, I believe you signed it.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, last night, did you have a chance to review this document in total before you did sign it?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And does this document accurately reflect what you said during the course of these interviews?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I asked you the questions that -- or if I asked you about the information set forth in this document here in the courtroom today, would your answers be the same as that set forth in the statement before you?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: They would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we'd like to offer into evidence 1D00-0750.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in principle we have no objection. But we just received the statement in the cross-examination material. We didn't receive it last night after it was completed. I think the statement goes beyond normal cross-examination documents, and, you know, in the future if this is going happen, we would ask that we get as much notice as possible of a 92 ter statement being submitted by the Defence through a witness like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, there's some parallel and some similarity with proofing notes, that is, statements taken after the arrival of a witness. I would say it would be -- the Chamber has some difficulties in immediately deciding upon the matter not only because Ms. Gustafson has not fully digested the document, but also because the Chamber usually wants to know what it admits into evidence. And we have seen it now for, I think one minute, which is not sufficient for 11 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm shocked, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is becomes exhibit number D1217.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1217 is marked for identification, and the chamber would to like receive a hard copy, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that even -- that we can follow better and even put an eye on the document when the witness testifies. The problem is that if finally, for whatever reason, we would not admit it, that, of course, would highly influence the course of the cross-examination, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, we are a bit -- and I have no reason at this moment to expect that we would not admitted it into evidence, but we just haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed on the basis as if this document would be admitted into evidence. We expect, Mr. Boucher, that we might not finish this morning, and that your testimony could be concluded only this afternoon, which gives us at least some additional time for reading during the breaks. Let's proceed on this basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. One of my colleagues is going to get a hard copy. At this point, I will be referring to various paragraphs as we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have it on our screen for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher, I would like to direct your attention to the statement given to the Gotovina Defence yesterday. And I would like to talk to you a little bit about some of the items that I believe you started to get into during the course of direct -- and Ms. Gustafson had a different question for you. But -- and in paragraph 9 of the statement that you gave to the Defence, you talk to some degree about your early impressions in Sector South, concerning -- and this is prior to Operation Storm, Mr. Boucher. Concerning abandoned and burnt houses that you observed. Can you just give the Chamber a bit of an idea of your impressions on that line.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, this being my first UN mission, in 2001 I also worked in Kosovo, which was prior to this statement. But before going to Croatia, as I mentioned, there was briefings on what to expect. Also about the role of UN civilian police, that the conflict was between two groups. The comments was, Once you're in a monitoring role, you really have to stay impartial as best you can. And there was even comments -- and I'm saying this because it leads to how I entered these -- from Zagreb, Zagreb and on to the Sector South. To stay impartial because you're surrounded by certain groups of people who have basically the control of this area, and you will be monitoring what is happening there. There were comments like, Make sure you don't fall into a Stockholm syndrome by the people around you. Try to see both sides of the arguments, try to negotiate, bringing two sides together, and so on. But upon physically entering -- well, first of all, in Zagreb a little bit more briefing about what to except in whole, and first of all, I finally find out I was going to Sector South, as opposed to another sector. There would be briefing even on the spot, and that's why I was stationed at first at the station in Drnis to understand how Zone of Separation works, and so on. So I knew this in Zagreb. When I entered the Sector South, after several days of delays because of road conditions and so on, it's in January and the roads were in very good shape, you're hit by, visually, seeing a lot of house that were burnt, you know, obviously vacant. There was no roofs on them, and they were -- this was the result what I found out in Zagreb, in Ottawa, and also by -- once in the sector, this was the result of destruction that took place in 1991, in the start of this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now can you give us a time-frame of when you're first seeing this, and are in the Serb-held territory of the Krajina, when you see this?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Right. Well, I arrived, I think it's in mid-January in Zagreb. Briefing, it took about five or six days. I was ready to go, but just the road condition was not very good. So it would be closer to the end of January by the time I finally entered the sector. It was explained to me, you're entering a sector, a so-called Krajina - I still don't know what that means - but that's what the Serb rebels - is the way I would them who had control. The Serb rebels had control of this territory, but also, there was also three other territories, or three other sectors, if you want. I also saw a lot of destruction which was left over from 1991. But also saw very well traffic, again, because there is lack of fuel for a lot of people moving about, especially in the rural area. It seemed like a very depressed area. I mean, it hits you when you come from large cities with all kinds ever things and traffic and moving about and jobs and whatever. A lot of things were a little bit behind from -- of course, from Canada, where I was used to seeing big farm machinery, for example, you're dealing with small areas and horse-drawn, and I, as I mentioned earlier today, a lot of people would actually be moving with these little tractors that you sit in the wagon, so it looks like a very depressed area. A lot of long faces also. People who I guess had lived through this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me cut through this.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During the period of time I think you had, you know -- if you hadn't said this previously. I mean, you tried to talk to both sides, tried to talk to Croats, tried to talk to Serbs that were in the area; did you not?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I did once I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And on that score, did you begin to learn things about what happened prior to Operation Storm, obviously concerning the Croat population and the continued harassment of the Croat population?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That was quite evident, and there was a lot of situational reports that would identify this. But in order to get both sides of the coin, as I mentioned earlier, from the orientation in Ottawa, you could not listen only to the Serb in the so-called Krajina. You had to listen to the Croats on the other side. And understanding fully well, this is Croatia, with rebel areas. So to understand both sides, you have to talk to somebody. And on the Croatian side, which I didn't spend very much time, because my main duty was in Sector South. On the Croatian side, I had many discussions with police officers who were police officers but before 1991, Croatian police officers. And some of them were actually thrown in jail by the group of rebels, by some of them who were actually their co-workers, their co-police officers, and so on. So you get the feeling of what exactly happened around 1991, when really, the rebel Serbs did not want to wear the insignia, the chequer board insignia of Croatia on their police hats. And so that was the start of it. The other thing is, made very clear to me, the former Yugoslavia only had one army for the whole Yugoslavia, and the army was controlled by the Serb. The Croatian side, when they separated, the only way they prevented a full sector, if you want, a complete sector of Croatia, was by police officers with small arms, pistols and shotguns, and so on, and maybe some civilians also, they prevented the whole take over, if you want, of Croatia in this conflict. So if you listen to this side -- not to take sides of the Croats or down play the Serb situation, but that's the situation that I had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you went in there, was there a degree of frustration on the Croatian side of the status quo with the zone of separation?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Very much so, on may fronts. One was right in the Zone of Separation of several areas. There were cemeteries, and actually both sides wanted to -- this is something a bit unique. There is an high esteem, if you want, on cemeteries and the dead, and they really want to visit their dead, families and so on, and that became a conflict for us in the UN, particularly the military side, to allow them to go there for their ceremony, and so on. And then who could go through the Zone of Separation. And then the mining that took place, you know. I think both sides put mines to protect their side, and then the UN tried to take control in the centre. It was quite -- quite a task just to try to control that, although it wasn't the responsibility of the civilian police. We had to travel through the Zone of Separation continuously. As far as frustration, yes, there was a lot of frustration because when I arrived four years later, there was really no progress, from both sides. And they are frustrated with the UN. As I had said before, we were visitors there trying to keep the peace, if you can, in our case monitoring, which is not really keeping the peace. And for me very frustrating because this was a mission where I was not armed, could not even defend myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just get back -- with regard to the frustration, let's just talk about the Croat side. I mean, you heard stories from the Croat side of relatives and loved ones being abused inside the Krajina, and you, likewise, heard that there was a frustration about the UN not doing anything. That frustration was at its peak during the time you got there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I'm just pausing for the interpretation. Now, that frustration, did that make things difficult in post-Operation Storm, certainly the relationship between the Republic of Croatia authorities after they came in and the UN?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It did for CIVPOL for sure. It did for a lot of the other -- the other agencies. I won't speak for them. They can speak on their own. But for CIVPOL, they saw us as police officers from many countries, and they were hoping that we would be able to solve what should have been police matters, seniors being assaulted, theft happening from them, phone calls, threatening phone calls, and things like this, when, in fact, we were only monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: These are threats and phone calls against the Croatian population prior to Operation Storm, right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Against the minority Croats that there were, left in the sector, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you noted during the course of your direct examination that during the period of time that the area was held by the Krajina Serbs, there was also a black market?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
