utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the black market brings with it a criminal element, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It does. There is a contrabands going through different routes, through Bosnia, a lot of it going all the way to Serbia, and that's the word from interpreters as much as locals. I mean, there's goods being transported back into the -- and obviously, going around Zones of Separation or other means. I don't know how exactly they made it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As a police officer for 30-odd years, sir, you're familiar with the black market and the criminal element. And you're likewise familiar with -- with or know that what comes with that often times is violence.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not that black market continued to exist after Operation Storm there?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Was no need for black market after this. Because the Croats, if you went outside of the Zone of Separation, whether it be Split, Sibenik Zagreb, any community outside of these sectors, there were plenty of goods to be bought, to be imported from other countries, and so on. So there was no ration for fuel, for clothing, and food, and so on. And as soon as the Zone of Separation disappeared, it was a free-flowing market for everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Along that black market score, I mean, prior -- prior to Operation Storm, did you learn of violence among black marketeers and criminals just among the Serb population before Storm?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes. It is obviously a matter of greed, which is typical, even on our streets. Where there's different groups that compete for the territory, for anything that's being sold, from drugs to fire-arms to any goods. So that existed. There was -- I don't want to talk about rumours, because it is non-proven. But there is rumours of different groups trying to control what came in and how it came in, and tried to prevent others from doing the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And these rumours that you heard about groups controlling the black market and preventing others from doing it, did those rumours include that individuals were killing other individuals in order to control those areas?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Again, they're rumours. Not -- we didn't investigate that per se, to say we have information on that, so, again, they're rumours at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let's turn our attention to the time just before Operation Storm. You did see, just prior to Operation Storm, an increase in ARSK troop movements, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you noted in -- at paragraph 6 in your statement to the Gotovina Defence that the rebel Serbs, however, did not want to become part of Croatia. Now this morning, just going on that line, this morning, when you were asked some questions about the evacuation or people leaving by Ms. Gustafson, and this is at page 15, line 11. You don't have that before you, but just for the court's reference. You started to say: It actually started before that, again, going back to, and then you were cut off. So let's me allow you to elaborate on what you began during direct, concerning the departure of the Serb population prior to Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, there is two events that really shattered the confidence of the rebel Serbs, and whoever could leave, probably tried to leave or wanted to leave or left. The first event was when the Croat army took Sector West in, I don't know, five or six hours, it was over. They realize a few things, and again --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who is the they, when you say "they?"

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: The Serb rebels realized that the Yugoslav army and Serbia is not behind us, to help us, which was one belief that they always it. If we need help, Big Brother will come and help. And it went, destroyed this statement heard many times, wherever there is one Serb, it's Serbia. So that shattered that approach. The second thing that really -- so a lot of people starting to leave. You could see some people were organising their trips and I had heard all kinds of stories about this after the 1st of May. And some left to go outside. The second event was when the rebel Serbs fired -- I think they're called --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Orkan rockets?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yeah. Some kind of bombs that shatters and throws all kinds of pieces. When they then fired this into Zagreb on the square, and it hit - actual killed people but injured other people - it was reported in the local paper, the Slobodna Dalmatia, that now, that irritated the Croats, but it also put on the heels a lot of people that lived there, the rebel Serbs, to say, Are we rattling the cage here, and what will happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before you move on, do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you're using the interpreter "rebel Serbs" in various contexts. If it is about firing rockets, then I understand that it's the Serb military who takes up arms against the Croatians. But you also used that term in the context of wanting to leave, where it seems to me that you're referring rather to the Serb population of the area, and I do not know on what basis you consider the whole of the population to be rebels or just people residing there and perhaps wanting to leave. That's -- so could you -- when you used the expression "rebel Serbs," could you always be clear to whom exactly you refer, because in the question, Mr. Kehoe was referring to the Serb population, which is, of course, not the same as active members of the ARSK, the armed force of the republic Republic of the Serbian Krajina, perhaps those who were -- who actively and positively joined the armed forces and perhaps others who were -- who had to, but mainly because they were living there. So it is a quite a complex concept you're talking about, and I would like to -- I would invite you to always make clear exactly what you're referring to, instead of using rebel Serbs. Not to say that there would be or would be no merit in considering Serbs, whether all Serbs or some of the Serbs to be rebels against the Croatian government. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can maybe clear why that statement comes out like this. First of all, all the men who would be of probably driving age except very old men, were provided with camouflage were provided with AK-47s, were provided with grenades, training. So all the men between 18 and, I think, 60 or maybe even 65, were considered and were enlisted to be part of the Krajina Defence system, if you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has heard quite some evidence on that aspect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may just clarify an issue - thank you, Mr. President. If I may clarify one issue. You noted that another event that caused concern among the Krajina Serbs was the shelling of Zagreb, and you were going to describe what you knew about the -- what weapon system was used. Do you recall what it was used?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, the word used was "cluster bombs." So in other words, when land, they throw projectiles, and I think they're made to injure people or kill them. But it's not just one -- one piece that stays together as a projectile, but it sort of throws a lot of projectile. And, again, I'm not a military person, but the military that were around me were telling me that cluster bombs were -- if you hit a crowd, you're going to kill a lot of people. That's the idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On the 4th, or thereafter of August during Operation Storm, did you see the HV firing any such weaponry, such cluster bombs like that?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let's move back to the two events you talked about, the fall of Sector West and also the shelling of Zagreb, and that was in the first week of May, the end of the first week of May, 1995. Was it not?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I think it was on the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's move ahead. And what was the temperature, if you will, as it grew in the Krajina thereafter?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Temperature about the feeling of people and so on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: The panic was starting to set in, as I mentioned before. One -- they felt there was no backing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm just trying to fix the microphone. It's hard to believe somebody can't here me, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They, the Krajina Serbs, felt there is no backing or no Big Brother to come and help them should they need help. The other things is they also realize that they were well trained, the Croatian army was well trained or well planned, if you want, directed or whatever -- sorry. Whatever the comments was, and that's sort of scared them. Because a lot of them who were in 1991 knew that didn't exist then. And, again, I'm reporting what I had heard from the locals. And then after this, again was -- which happened, I think, it was in June or something when the shelling to Zagreb happened, which another month or even more than a month later, so, again, that's -- a lot of them were starting to panic. If we don't have Big Brother behind us, a solid, larger military force, we won't be able to defend ourselves. And this is something I actually discussed with the chief of the milicija at the time, Mr. Vojko. I made it plain to him, like, if a confrontation happens, do you think you can defend yourself with this old stuff you have here, like old vehicles, and his comment is, Don't worry about us. So again, I'm not a military man, but it is it pretty obvious that when have you vehicles dating bark to just after World War II, you know, how are you going to compete with a modern military?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continuing on that score, up until the -- after the shelling of -- of Zagreb and through Operation Storm, were people continuing to leave?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now -- I'm sorry, were you going to add something?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes. The other aspect, was for us, for UN CIVPOL at that point, I also had discussion with the commissioner of CIVPOL in Zagreb, and I said, You know, as CIVPOL monitors and their mission, they usually go through Zagreb to either fly to their home country or somewhere else on holidays, maybe it would be wise not to send new monitors that are coming on to mission to Sector South. And we reduced a number of UNCIVPOL monitors by a large number. In other words, when Storm happened, we were down to about two dozen, and before that, we were about 200. So we ourselves adjusted to some of this comments that we heard regularly. And by the way, a lot of people think that even the locals and that could be Croats, or Serb, in this Krajina, a lot of people thought they weren't well-informed, but they were well-informed. They had contacts with families in other places, which some of them auto used to live there and are displaced, you know, around 1991 when the conflict started. And the local paper was always brought in by somebody, and TV, by the way, there was two stations that played regularly, just with simple rabbit ears on the TV, you could catch a Croat channel and a Serb channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By the way, If I can ask you just an aside. I'm going back to Sector West which you mentioned previously. Were you aware that the UN had assisted at the request of the ARSK government, that the UN assisted removing Serbs from Sector West in an operation called Operation Safe Passage? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I had heard about it, but I don't know who the principal was, who took charge, and who did what.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's talk about the fall of Grahovo the 28th of July, 1995. You recall that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: No -- I don't, what Grahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When the HV began to make incursions up on the Dinara?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now that was at the end of July; was it not?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It was ongoing for quite a long time because they were actually, from what we were told through UN briefings, the Croat army was actually making a road to bring equipment in Dinara mountain, which is actually a fairly steep mountain, a lot of rocks. So it was ongoing for a long period of time, and the UN was monitoring this through, I don't know what means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you aware at the end of July that President Martic of the Republic of Serbian Krajina had declared war or had declared a state of war? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I don't recall this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. But you were aware that the HV was possessed on the Dinara to take Knin and the Krajina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: The comments that -- we had briefings, by the way, every morning, which was main agencies together, including the military commander for the UN, CIVPOL, UNHCR, I forget, but many agencies. Every morning we would try to report some of the things we found, where we're going and, you know, things like this. So I was aware that this was happening, and I was also informed that, you know, one of the comments that came -- and if I remember right, it came from Colonel Leslie, there's 10.000 soldiers, Croatian soldiers, just waiting to come in. So it reached a point, they're right beside Knin, not very far. So from this point, it was obvious that if there is 10.000 soldiers -- I do not believe there was 10.000 soldiers, but there was maybe a few thousand soldiers. Irregardless, in my mind, in police terms, and I'm sure military terms would be the same, you cannot keep 1.000, never mind any more, sitting still, feeding them, bedding them, and making sure they're, you know, ready for a long period of time. Something will happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So in your mind, Mr. Boucher, it wasn't a matter of if the HV was going to move. It was simply a matter of when.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And prior to Operation Storm when the HV was sitting up on the Dinara, they were not shelling Knin on -- until the morning of the 4th, were they?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: They were not. Can I just add one other point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It's a point of interest, because there was discussions between the president, President Tudjman, and Milosevic at the high level to see if they finally break a deal. It was happening at the same time, and I'm sorry, I do not remember where it was, whether it was Brussels or somewhere else. But the locals - and so was I - were following then, and it was about the same time, it was in July, end of July, beginning of August. And finally they both walked away. There was no deal. So from that point. I can tell you the arms went down from a lot of people thinking, What's next?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the population continued to leave, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us talk about this particular period of time. It is this time, and I think you referred to this in paragraph 33 of the statement that you gave to the Defence. Where you note on the eve of Storm. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll let you catch up.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "On the eve of Storm I had a conversation with General Forand, and he said that the Serbs should have an escape plan, or at least think about one. This was not to give Mr. Vojko a tip, but really just to say that unless he didn't care about the people that stood by him in the protests not to be part of Croatia, he should help them. The attempt was to save lives. They could have prepared an escape route ..." Now you discussed just earlier about you going down to see Mr. Vojko, and I trust that is the conversation that you were discussing. But the general consensus, Mr. Boucher, was that the HV, in time, had the ability to surround Knin, cut it off, and destroy it. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's right. In my mind, it was, and I would add that the -- the discussion with the General Forand was in the morning in one of the briefing, and he asked me, Could you please at least ask him if he has a plan? And that was the intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Because -- because the general idea from General Forand and from you was that if Knin was surrounded, and if the HV moved in in force to attack, there would be an extremely high casualty rate among the people living in Knin. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Potential was very, very high, unless everybody put their hands in the heir. But if they were fighting for that territory for four years, we had no idea what exactly they could do. Just one last point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: There was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I was waiting for the translation, but you go ahead.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Sorry. There was a lot of senior people, too, that were not mobile, and there were some that did not want to be mobile.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me go back to an answer that you gave. And when I gave you the scenario of a massive urban conflict, that the only way out was a bloody conflict or put their hands up. Was there any indication that you saw prior to Operation Storm that the RSK authorities were planning on putting their hands up and saying, We give up?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: No indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After the attack ensued on the morning of the 4th, of 1995, did you receive any information prior no the artillery salvo on the 5th, that the ARSK wanted to contact the HV and say, We give up?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in General Forand and your attempt to avoid a bloody urban battle, you wanted Vojko to plan an escape route out; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In rejecting your entreatise, did Vojko tell you that the RSK and the ARSK were planning for a last ditch stand in Knin?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: He did not mention that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And as you learn about how things ensued with the attack on Operation Storm, you concluded, did you not, that the planning by the HV and General Gotovina to allow that escape route was the humanitarian thing to do because it avoided an urban bloody conflict. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: This is what happened. What the planning was, who planned, I'm sorry, I wasn't part of, I don't know. But it was obvious that there was a route leading towards Sector North and Topusko with hundreds of people moving that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn your attention, if we can, to the actual shelling of Knin. And if we could bring back up on the screen, if I may, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, could I ask one or two additional questions, because -- You describe that people were leaving through what you considered to be escape routes. Now, the question was that this was part of General Gotovina's plans to leave them open and to -- what's the basis -- and you more or less -- in your answer, you describe the situation, whereas the answer was specifically not on what you saw happening but whether you were aware that that was part of the plan of General Gotovina. Now, do you have any knowledge about what you saw on the ground being part of the plan by General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have any knowledge about the plan to attack and take Knin, nor leaving escape routes going anywhere other than the fact that I know people -- the word got around among themselves, this is the route to go. And within hours, I remember after I was back at the UN headquarters, speaking with the commander, UNCIVPOL commander or Sector Chief in Sector North saying, They are coming our way, the refugees leaving your territory, your Sector South. But I do not know who was part of the plan or what the plan was from a military point of view. No idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I could have asked a similar question on 50 per cent of the topics you dealt with at this moment. I heard no objections about laying a foundation and source of knowledge. But even if there's no objection, that doesn't mean that it is not relevant for the Chamber to hear the source of knowledge, and that it would not be important for the Chamber that a foundation is laid. And from this last answer, you see what was more or less intertwined observations on what happened on the ground and what were the plans, that you skillfully have woven them together in your questions, and the witness has confirmed and responded in the affirmative to your questions. But upon further examination, it turns out he has - which doesn't come as a surprise - no knowledge whatsoever of at least part of you put to him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On that score, just staying with that last answer, Mr. Boucher, you do know that the HV did not cut off that escape route. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let's turn to the shelling of Knin, sir, and if we could go back to the 1179 -- actually, the second photograph of the blow-up that you made marks on. Now, Mr. Boucher, this is the photograph, the little blow-up that you had written on this morning, and I'd like to talk first about your particular residence. And from your particular residence, you are familiar with the ARSK barracks are you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And approximately how far was your residence from the military barracks?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: From my residence to about the entrance gate to the north barracks, I would estimate about 500 feet. It's not far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, also in that general area was the milicija. And the milicija, I believe during the course of your statements said that's the police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, could you with a blue pen on this particular document, then we'll have to put another item, but could you circle in blue pen with the number 1 next to it, where the milicija is.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Have I no objection, Your Honour. It's just that this location was marked on the other photo as B, if we want to use the same letter, that's fine. If not, that's fine too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the precisions and corrections could use the same agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine -- can we remove that, and we can put the letter B, as opposed to the number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The letter B?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you make a cross and a letter B, then we know that the circles are for the Prosecution, and the crosses are for the Defence in different colours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll put a cross on it, and I'll write B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, would you mind if the witness also marks where the entrance gate is, because it could be far closer if the entrance gate is at an odd position. Could you mark also where the entrance gate is that you just referred to, and we have no entrance gate yet. So if you would make that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I made an X.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, X is -- yes. The X is where it is, and then if you could put a letter to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we want to stay with this, it's N.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: N is the next ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now again from your residence, how far is the milicija?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It would be about the same distance, about 500 feet and so on. Three's blocks are actually only the thickness of a house, so it is not really -- so I would say 500 feet, maybe. I don't think it is more than 600 feet. Not far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's talk about the milicija and this being the police headquarters. Is this where you met Mr. Vujko?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And tell us a little bit about the role of the milicija as an entity of the police and also as having military functions.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, this was a learning experience for me in this mission, where police officers could change their identity from being civilian police officers to military. In other words, there would be many times during the time before Operation Storm where all of the milicija, Serb police, would change from their blue uniform of police, civilian police, to green. And I had asked interpreters and people who lived in town why was that. And for one thing -- one answer was a lot of these people are actually -- they were not police officers before 1991. They became police officers because they didn't want to go to the front where the military where positioned, but in case of emergency or certain training, they were all included as part of this, again, so-called Krajina area defence system, or military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you become aware, Mr. Boucher, that prior to Operation Storm and during Operation Storm members of the milicija had been sent to the front line on the Dinara?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to the time or the day or night just before Operation Storm, and I want to direct your attention to paragraph 34 of -- of your statement. In paragraph 34 of your statement, you note -- this is the second sentence: "The night before Storm was actually very, very quiet. I know that because I woke at maybe 2.00 in the morning. I was on the second floor and could hear people talking in the field in the back, so I got up. Of course I couldn't see anything, but I could hear them running through the bushes. In retrospect I believe it was probably Croatian soldiers in the middle of the night looking at the area where they were going to attack and maybe figuring out distance -- figuring out distance for their guns." Now before I ask you about this specific incident, as a police officer for many years and with the RCMP and with the police in Medicine Hat, it's typical for you as a police officer before you do a radio or an arrest or a search to go get real time information of that location just before you send police in; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It is. It's very accurate, even more so if it was a SWAT team. You want to know the doors, the windows, the exits, the potential getaway systems, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now when this happened on the early mourning hours of the 4th, you thought it was essentially the same thing but in a military context, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I didn't think this at 2.00 or 3.00 in the morning, but by the morning when the first shell was fired, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When that first shell was fired, you concluded they were down there trying to get real time information?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now as we move back through the particular shelling, and if we can go back to the exhibit that's on the screen, and I want to take you to paragraph 36 of your statement, and also, actually, it begins, if I may, on paragraph 16 of your 2008 statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. That would be P1178. At paragraph 16, you note that at paragraph 40 of my 1999 statement, I mentioned that one shell went through my roof. I think they were aiming at the ARSK and milicija building." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you concluded that, sir, when you went in your basement and you thought about the direction of fire and the location of those targets, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell us what you did.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I also thought that maybe because the owner of this house was an older man, Serb man about 75, his son in law was also an officer in the ARSK. It was either a house target for this, to get back at this officer. Or what was maybe more plain, because as you see in the picture, it is fields behind my house. I thought that any other shell that doesn't make it to the north barracks or the milicija office, I'm in danger here. And particularly -- because I went to the basement. In the basement of the window, right in front where I was sitting, because it is a small basement, so then at that point, I realized, I better get out of here because of all of the shells that are coming in, if one another one misfires, and doesn't reach the anticipated target, it might be the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the direction of fire was coming over your house towards the military barracks?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: From all the plans that I had seen in the UN briefings and where the soldiers were waiting on Dinara mountain, I was in the -- pretty well the direct line to the north barrack and also milicija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And is that what caused you in paragraph 36 of your statement to the Defence to say: "As I said, I'm not a military man. When the shelling began, it became obvious that the shelling was geared towards the military compound." Do you see that as the first sentence?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- questions being asked on the Defence statement, that it be more appropriate to be asked in a non-leading way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's cross-examination I would say under Rule 90 (H), where the Defence considers that the witness may have knowledge which would support the Defence case, which is, of course, not the typical type of cross-examination where you challenge the evidence which was elicited by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I must demure in the sense that many of the witnesses that we have -- have been put on by the Prosecution were witnesses that we were, in fact, using to get information to support the Defence. Much in the same way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is a part -- that may be true. That is not an answer to how you should examine those witnesses when you are not challenging the evidence they gave to the Prosecution, but where you are seeking to elicit evidence which supports your own case, but I do see that it's not always easy to draw that line. But in view of my earlier question I put to the witness and the short comment I gave on that, I would say that it would certainly assist the Chamber if would you follow the suggestion as is implied in Ms. Gustafson's observation or objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may just on that score, Your Honour, I mean, we are, in fact, challenging the position of the Prosecution through this witness. I mean -- the picture that the Prosecution is trying to develop through this witness is countered directly from the questions that I'm asking on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, therefore, Rule 90 (H) isn't even needed, isn't it? Should I give you an opportunity to read the three small notes that Mr. Misetic passed to you? I will give you an opportunity to do that if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't need them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't need them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I say this, with all due respect, Mr. Misetic, I'm sorry about that. What I'm saying to you is that they led evidence on shelling, specific evidence on shelling that we are challenging through this witness, and this is the -- this is a direct challenge to it, and that's why I submit to the Chamber that this is appropriate for leading questions on cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was a simple challenge to the evidence, and there would be no need to take a separate statement eliciting new positive assertions from this witness. The Defence has done that, and if they're going ask questions about those assertions, I think it should be done --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could also be, Ms. Gustafson, a matter of efficiency to put already -- if you expect that cross-examination would take quite sometime, to put it on paper. So the mere fact that it appears in this statement as such is not a reason to follow your suggestion. I think the views on both sides have been expressed clearly, and I would suggest that you keep in the back of your mind, Mr. Kehoe, what I said had some merit and Ms. Gustafson's observations, and that we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I will attempt to negotiate that with as non-leading questions as I possibly can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the direction of fire, let us talk about the time that the firing commenced. The firing commenced at 5.00 a.m. in the morning. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Boucher, it commenced at a time when there was virtually no one on the streets. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you moved to the location from A to D, and then you went to the location which is F. And I believe you said that there was a -- another building, G, that had also received a round.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now that, sir, was in a line of fire of the ARSK facility that you see before you, marked as the Knin general Supply. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Approximately how far was the -- it's been known as the Senjak barracks during the course of this trial, so approximately how far is F from the entry or the Senjak barracks as a whole?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I would say no more than about 200 feet, 250 feet at the max. It's not far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you were running from A to D, and then from D to F, did you see any dead bodies on the street?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you asked about the damage to building D, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: G. I think I was talking about G.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: G.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Isn't that G there? Isn't that above F is G? That's what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, you were talking about that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think he said during direct that G had taken a round.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: G had a hole on the side of the building about two metres in diameter, big one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you both for G and for D, could you mark on this map - and it has not yet been stored, I think - could you mark on the map the direction of the impact, which means that if you give it a small arrow that the point of the arrow is at an angle of 90 degrees to the wall that was hit. Do you understand what I mean? If this is the wall, that the arrow points at that wall at 90 degrees which is not to say that the wall was hit under that same angle, but at least we know on which side of the building that wall was found. Could you do that for D and for G.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Same colour, blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blue. Yes, that is fine. The Chamber borrows the colour. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I think it is it appropriate to have your own colour. I'm kidding. Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Boucher, when you look back at these events, for instance, the firing on your house, did you conclude that -- that they were firing on the barracks, and they just missed, or fired on some other military targets and just missed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that the source of the witness's knowledge of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Targeting be explored, if these questions are going to be asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's look at the question very precisely. Well, the question is a factual one, whether the witness concluded or not. What the value of such conclusions is, is, of course, a different matter. So it's -- you may answer that question, whether you concluded that or not, Mr. Boucher, if you drew such a conclusion, it might be good for us to know on what specific knowledge or expertise you based that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I mentioned before, I am not an expert in military large weapons. I happen to be -- was the best shooter in the RCMP in all of Canada. Won the Canuck Cup which is a competition. It's in the small arms, but understanding projectile as they pushed through powder or explosives, some of them misfire, some of them have delayed firing, and the accuracy of shooting depends a lot on the competence of the shooter and the equipment. So if I leave it with this, in my mind, I have seen rounds with a pistol or rifle that didn't go as far as the previous round with the same weapon, and I have seen ones that didn't fire. I have seen one that were delayed reaction, and I sent a total of six years as an instructor for all the RCMP in the basic training, and I have seen millions of rounds, but it is in small-arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you drew any conclusions, I take it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Or thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or thereafter, and, if so, on what this conclusion was based.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And in my statement, Your Honour, I indicated that I believe that the rounds were not making it to the intended targets of the northern barracks or the milicija office. That's what in my mind because I was so close to them, and I have -- I had walked in front of them. I have seen military equipment around. I have seen the police turn into military, the Serb police milicija. And I was almost positive in my mind that the intention of the Croatian army was to hit those targets. But the rounds did not make it, and one of them hit my house, one of them hit a house very close to mine. And, again, the house where the two CIVPOL colleagues were also living was also hit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, on what was your assumption based that, as you said, that the intention was to hit the targets you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I knew where the positions of the Croatian army was on Dinara mountain, and it leads backwards from the arrow that I showed on the -- on the map. So it was pretty obvious at this point and after that the rounds being shot were coming this way, and particularly again -- and I wasn't thinking about the -- the military compound which is called general supply, Knin general supply. I completely forgot about that. In my mind, the only thing I could think is they are trying to hit the northern barracks and the milicija office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me put it very bluntly to you. It's the Prosecution's position that the targeting was intended to or -- as a matter of fact, that it was indiscriminate fire. Did you have any knowledge, or do have you any -- because your whole reasoning appears to be based on, I would say, decent military targeting, which is the position of the Defence as well. Now the position of the Prosecution is a totally different one. Now your reasoning is apparently based on a decent military targeting concept. Is there any reason why you would know whether the Defence is right in its position that it was decent military targeting or whether the Prosecution is right in their position, that it was incriminate shelling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only my sheer deduction that if you are in a combat situation, and that could be police as much as military, you will try to neutralise your enemy or your opponent fairly quick. And for them, it would be to try to neutralize the northern barracks in this case or the milicija, which were actually potential conflict for them or confrontational for them, because they had personnel, equipment, and so on. From Dinara mountain with long binoculars or telescope, I'm sure they could see where the equipment was, you know, large vehicles, trucks, and so on, they're green, so they're, you know, easy to spot, and they were really the only ones that were moving around, as far as large equipment. This is a deduction on my part, but if I was in a confrontation, as a police officer, it would be the same thing. Try to neutralize the conflict as soon as you can that poses the most dangerous potential to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me take you through your path of going from A to D to F. And before I ask you that, you knew, sir, based on information that you received that if shelling ensued you were instructed to get down, don't move around, and go into a low place, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: This is something I learned from Colonel Leslie. And it happened maybe three or four weeks before, because I had never thought about this, but Colonel Leslie said, If ever there is shelling, lay low, go in a basement somewhere, don't run the streets, because have you more chances of getting killed by pieces of pavement flying than the projectile itself, so debris will kill you, cement or whatever, so lay low. So based on that, that's why I laid low for two hours in the basement of my rented accommodation, and when I realized it was wasn't as safe, or certainly not as safe as it should have been, I moved across the street to the other house that had a large foundation, if you want, or a basement, no windows. And then from there, I was the Sector Chief. So I had to find my way back to the UN as best as I could, which, by the way, the UN had sent an APC to pick me up twice, and they went to my house, saw the big hole in the roof and thought I had -- I was done. And twice I walked out of this second house because I heard this large noise, like a loud truck, if you want, loud motors, and I don't even know if it has a muffler on it. But by the time I would come out of that second house basement, I could see the white UN APC driving away. So by the second time I realized they are probably not coming back to pick me up. I am going to have to move.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, staying with the early part of your answer, did Colonel Leslie, or did anybody in the UN tell you that, The purpose of artillery is to suppress movement of troops or people or anybody else?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It wasn't explained to that level, except for your answer safety we were supplied a fairly thick vest, a fairly heavy thick vest, and a blue hard helmet, but this has limited protection. The only comment was if there's shelling, don't run the streets, hide. And, in my mind, I knew with the -- from the plans or the maps that were shown where the Croatian army was stationed on mount Dinara, so I had to protect myself from that angle to stay behind some other larger buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you went to F, you, in fact -- F, the building that is circled with F, and i use that initial. When you went to that location, you went down to the basement, and the basement was populated with people, wasn't it, that he were laying low and not moving?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It -- it was pretty full of people that were from that building. And, again, it's a similar, the several similar buildings there. G is a the same type of building as F, and then there's other ones beside as you can see. All about five or six floors, I'm not sure. So I would think that the residents from those buildings were in the basement and -- and even people that came from other places to hide there because this was tactically probably a very safe building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were down in that basement, and you were done there for some hour, were you not?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were down in that basement, did the people in that basement tell you that neighbours and loved ones had been killed during the shelling?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I do recall that they were quite upset. Some of them who could speak English were saying, Stop them, and do something. And my only comment is just last week the Serbs were, through aircrafts, bombing Bosnia, and the UN didn't stop them there either. So how could I stop them today? How could I stop the Croatian army today? So it was a long, long day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I'm looking at the clock. We had an earlier first break. Could you find a suitable moment to break within the next couple of moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Boucher, when you gave your statement in 1996 and described these events, if those people in the basement had told you that family and friends had been killed by shelling, you would have included that in your 1996 statement and -- but it's not there. But that is something that you would have included. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I would think so. It think it would be important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So based on the fact of that importance and the fact that it's not there, you can now conclude that those people did, in fact, not say anything about family and neighbours being killed during the shelling, did they?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I don't recall anyone talking about family or for friends being killed during that time. It was more berating the UN, You're useless, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break and resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, in view of the time estimates, may I assume that you will finish your cross-examination in the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, at the risk of not losing these etchings, if I could move this into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D1218.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1218 is admitted into evidence. And I noted that Ms. Gustafson has no objections. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, can we flip back to the other photograph in this exhibit, as I do believe it is now a joint exhibit, of 1179.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher -- oh, I'm sorry. Mr. Boucher, talking about the area K, you were asked a question by Ms. Gustafson on page 10, beginning on line 22, and you don't have that before you, sir, I'm reading from the transcript, so bear with me. This was from earlier this morning. Mr. Boucher, just staying with that map for a moment, the location, the large circle you mark with K where it was, you labelled it as residential area where you saw a lot of damaged houses. "Are you able to estimate for the Court how many houses you saw in that area you marked as K? "Answer: It would have to be a guesstimate. I think it would be in the neighbourhood of eight to ten." Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I think there was how many damaged houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Damaged houses. I'm sorry. Damaged in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many houses you saw damaged in that area damaged you marked as K, and you answered, it would have to be a guesstimate. I think it would something in the neighbourhood of about eight to ten. Now putting aside the residence that you -- your residence and the other CIVPOL residence, you don't know when these other houses were damaged, do you?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Of my recollection, that day my house, the two CIVPOLs residences, and the first one that received the first shell in the morning, which is about -- not that far. Right at the corner of the next street, if you want, so not very far. So the rest of them, I see in the -- the damaged houses several days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if I can show you P228. And, sir, this is an UNCIVPOL assessment of damages that I believe was shown to you last night. Do you recall this, sir?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in this particular assessment of damage by -- and you know Mr. Steinar Hagvag, do you not?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And from this report, and had you a chance to review this report, you told the Office of the Prosecutor -- and I realize Mr. President that Your Honours don't have a copy of this, so I'm reading from a proofing note. And I will try to quote as accurately as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If do you it literally then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Literally, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The witness thought the report was relatively accurate based on his observations. Is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us shift gears, and I want to talk to you a little bit about some of the burning and looting after Operation Storm that you discussed in the statement with the Prosecutor, and you first talked about it in your 2008 statement, and it would be in paragraph 19 of your 2008 statement. That would be your last statement. Do you have that before you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is, for the record, P1178.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And your note there is that there was a big difference in the demeanor between the Croatian army soldiers and officers. My impression of the soldiers was that they were "yahoos" out for revenge. I got the impressions commanders did not have much control over lower ranks. Tell us a little bit about that, Mr. Boucher. Can you tell us the foundation for that statement?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Right after the -- in my opinion, had fairly good control of Knin and not having been outside of Knin, but from what I see from the UN camp and also on my visit into town on foot in the next day in the cars, and that's within a few days, they're out drink, they're drunk. Some of them are shooting in the air with their AK-47s. Some grenades are thrown because it is a lower bang, if you want, than if it was a large tank or I guess larger equipment. A lot of swearing and yelling. You could see there was no rank structure or at least insignias on their shoulders or arms. The fact that they are showing up at the gate -- that was right after they really took control. And, again, pointing their weapons all over the place. I mean, there is usually a port arms position to carry a weapon, so that it's always safe, pointed in a safe direction. That didn't take place. They were all over the place, pointing it, and towards us, and as they turn, you know, not being careful with it. They broke ranks to come to the gate to ask about family members or friends are they in here and so on. It did not appear like it was controlled, disciplined. And I didn't see that in the rank. The rank and files, the Sergeants and higher, the one that had ranks showing on their shoulders or arms or Colonel Zelic, for example, who showed up several times at the gate to try to negotiate certain things. It was always to the point, you know, well-organised. But the lower ranks for what I would put it, would be -- if it is not out of control, certainly -- I put the term "yahoo." That is my term, maybe it's not correct, but it is certainly not professional, not what you would expect of a professional military, but in reality this is a new military, in my mind. It is four years old, there are some probably very good soldiers in it, but from what I could see right there in front of me, the lower ranks, not very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me discuss some of the trips that you had made out of the base, and I think you weren't sure if it was the 6th or the 7th, but I think you said this morning it was the 7th. The first time you wept to your residence and it was looted, the only thing that was taken was beverages. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That I could see. I didn't stay there very long. One of the information I had from some of the military personnel, when you go back to certain places, watch out. Make sure there is no booby-traps or whatever it is, whatever that would be, is hidden wires, I guess, or whatever it may be. So I carefully went back into my accommodation, and I knew that just a few days before I had made a provision trip to make sure I had food in my house and I had bought a brand new case of Coca-cola, because it is in the summer, it's warm, and I put it in the fridge. That first visit, that was gone. I'll just retrace for a minute. For whatever reason, again, when the attack started, I went out of my residence after the shell, and I locked the door. And when I came back the door had been broken, the Coke is gone, but I can't see anything else missing. So that first visit, that's all I saw. It was only on the second visit -- of course, there is nobody in the house. On the second visit that I notice the TV is it gone. It's not my TV; it belonged to the owner of the house. But I had a brand new leather coat, which was not taken on the first visit I went back to my residence, but it was gone on the second one and so on. So there may have been waves of looting, if you want, to go and pick up whatever valuables was in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You don't know who went in there the second time and looted those other objects, do you?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Other than those who picked up the TVs, I didn't see them in my accommodation, but I saw them coming out of my houses close to mine with TVs and VCRs. Other than that, I don't know who else would have -- it could have been neighbours, if there was neighbours too. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By the way, I mean, staying with the TV sets and VCRs, and you mention this in your 1999 statement at paragraph 56 of the Puma brigade. "I saw a truck marked Puma Brigade. It had 50 to 60 TVs and VCRs." They were that openly, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you have any idea whether or not any of those items were inventoried after they were taken?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn our attention to the burning issue that you talked about on direct examination. And I believe in your first statement in 1996, if I may -- and that would be paragraph 10. You noted that there were three soldiers involved. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: If I wrote that in -- in -- closer to the event, I would say that that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just going back to the prior question on these TVs and VCRs. I asked you about inventory. Do you have any knowledge of whether or not the military police confiscated any of those items?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just -- if you could just refer to your first statement in paragraph 10. It notes that: "I saw a Croat truck Puma with cans of petrol and three soldiers burning houses on the road to Drnis."

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So this is three guys in a truck, and they had Puma on the truck?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was it spray painted on, was it --

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: All the ones that had Puma on it, were actually -- well, if it was painted or pasted on, but it was a clear-cut. It wasn't, like, just spray painted with a can type of thing. It was a clean indication of who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I mean, did you check for a plate, a licence plate?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: There was no licence plates on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, did this strike you as a sophisticated military operation, given some houses were burnt and others weren't, or did you believe this was three guys outdoing their own thing?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I can tell you that in 1995 and in 1996 and when I had to review this in 1999, I had a chance to review what exactly happened here. And in my mind, what I saw there is it looks like they're going systematic with cans they're going to be burning all these houses. And that's the statement I gave. But the more I thought about what happened what happened there in -- was why are there some houses not burnt? I started to question why is the process that they used, whoever they were, under what command, if there was any, to exempt some of them. I also started to put, maybe in my mind, two plus two here. I think there were some people who were out of control on their own. That's my feeling, because that can happen with the police, if there is no strict professional standards, policies, whatever it is. I also see some things that doesn't jive in my mind. And it's not just about the burning of houses, but why would they protect a Serb church if they want them out of there? I also saw that. So there were things that are just don't match to the original way I was thinking. I just thought, at first, they're cleaning house, and there's a really strong revenge to what happened to them, the Croats, in 1991. But there is a lot things that don't quite equal this. So in my mind, this is a young military, as I said, they recruited -- and some of them said that. They volunteered to take back their territory. What kind of training did they have, what kind of discipline did they have, did they have any ethic -- military ethic trainings? Those are things I would question -- I do question for a police officer. I think they would question that to say -- or did they just recruit people to have the numbers to do the attack and retake their territory. So that's -- the more I thought about it, I think there were a lot of people that weren't professional soldiers, and, of course, some of the things I listed to you, it was pretty easy for me with time to say, there was a bunch of people out of control here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying with this burning issue, sir, again, in your proofing statement with the Prosecution, you said that the witness remembered seeing "Hrvatska Kuca" written on houses. It didn't always make a difference to what happened to the house. Is that accurate, sir?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That is. There was -- they also would put [B/C/S spoken], don't touch. Hrvatska Kuca, meaning it was a Croat house. But even then, you see there was houses, the doors had been broken into. But some of this was also done quite a few days after, because what we started to notice is we had vehicles from outside of this so-called Krajina area, if you want, or Sector South, people who lived in Sibenik, Split, Zagreb came back, I think, to check on their houses or their relatives' house and whatever, and they spray painted that. That wasn't organised, I don't think, by any specific groups, because it was all kinds of different kinds of colours of paint and whatever. But it was done, and I think they were -- I would think they were trying to stop the looting or stop anybody damaging their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you also -- you noted in paragraph 42 of your statement to the Defence, D1217 MFI, that -- it's about three quarters of way down: "I also noted that there were Serb areas of some villages that were not burnt. Additionally, the Croat soldiers were escorting both Serb and Croat refugees to the UN compound, and General Cermak urged all Serbs to stay in Croatia. Further, Croatia appointed an ethnic Serb as the chief of police in Knin. I consider all these actions as inconsistent with the systematic attempt to keep Serbs from returning." I don't want to row hash what you put the statement, but are those some of the factors that have led to a reassessment of your position?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: This is -- these are some of the elements that don't match. If it was really organised to the point that everybody is on the same page under the same plan to do what -- I guess you would call ethnic cleansing, then I guess they would have flushed out everybody. But the reality is you mentioned some of the points. The other thing that is -- which I found out later. I didn't find out until several days after, is that we were notified that the attack was coming. So why would they do that if they really wanted to hide things, other than to prevent damages or death of UN personnel, and maybe -- and the timing, as you -- you mentioned that, but I think it makes sense, because in the police, we do the same thing. If you're going to do a search -- you want to surprise armed gangs, for example, you do it either in the middle of the night or really early in morning. There is an element of timing. So there is a lot of things about this that leaves you with the impression that I don't think everybody was on the same plan here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we have paragraph 42 on the screen. I'm sorry, Your Honour. General Cermak was mentioned in paragraph 42, and we don't have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's paragraph 42 of the Defence statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cermak is mentioned in the paragraph. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, no, no. That is not what I was reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not reading. Mr. Kay is apparently referring to the fact that Mr. Cermak appears in ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Remarkably, Your Honour, it is also paragraph 42 in the Defence statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So sorry, it's just that -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Matter is resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, by the way the Chamber would not mind if the balance between what the witness observed, questions about what he observed, and answers to what he observed, and how he developed over time his theories, his impressions, his opinions, et cetera, that could be a bit more in direction to the facts. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Consistent with what the President noted, can you give us the factual bases behind your conclusions during this, because, obviously, the Chamber wants to know if you have a conclusion, what facts led to you that conclusion. Whatever that conclusion happens to be concerning the situation that we were just discussing.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, I have to rely to my evidence and my experience, I guess, in my own sector. I'm a police officer, and for several years I used to do audits. And when you go and do that or verification in any office, you look for, Is everybody working on the same goals, on the same objectives. Who do you have working, doing what, and so on to achieve these goals so that you can measure that. Otherwise everything is doing their own thing, but there is no coercion. So policies, directives, and I don't have access to this, never did, for the Croat army. But I notice from my experience when you go do some offices, there is always some -- it seems like they are on their own agenda, their own -- you know, they make decisions on their own. It is always very important to have strong leadership at every level of supervision, and I would think in the military, it would probably be more important to have that. And I started to look at this, and I said, There is a lack of proper supervision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher, may I draw your attention to the difference of what a witness should tell a Court and what a police officer should investigate. I can imagine that a police officer seeks patterns in order to have access to other evidence, whereas a witness is primarily is expected to tell us about his personal observations, and I do see, and the Chamber does accept, that sometimes you can put it in a context on the basis of a wider set of information you have received, but the focus should be on your own observations. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just trying to go a step further from your prior question and try to lay out for the Chamber through the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the last answer was, again, very theoretical, and could you have stopped the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And just going back, the Chamber wants to know some of the facts that you're discussing. Let's go down to the next level. The facts that you're discussing that led to you a conclusion that what you observed was inconsistent with the systematic attempt to keep Serbs from returning.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Again, there are houses that are not burnt. They're Serb houses. So some obviously have a house to stay and maybe a field and a crop to collect. Mr. Cermak publicly - because when he came to the camp, the UN camp - publicly with the media there said Serbs that want to stay can stay. You know, the chief of police is a Serb. That's appointed. That in itself shows something. So there are things -- and, again, the Orthodox church are still standing, I think, as far as I know. Well, contrary, the Catholic -- so, I'm sorry, but these are the evidence that I saw that makes me think this one way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just staying with the -- the lack of destruction to the Orthodox church, and we talked about cemeteries before, that there was a -- first, that there was an effort not to have Orthodox churches damaged. Did you ever conclude that there was an effort not to have those graves desecrated as well?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: This is where I have a hard time understanding this. Because in my discussion with the policija and in the letter to Mr. Cermak, I'd asked for free movement to go everywhere, and although on paper it was afforded, in reality on the ground, it wasn't present. So that's why it doesn't jive. If we are monitors and we should be able to go everywhere, why are we not permitting? As far as -- just going back to the church, yes, the churches were protected. Right away. The soldiers were standing on guard, so that nobody would destroy them. And later it became police officers standing in front of the Orthodox church so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you allowed to go into the Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: No. Well, I never tried either. I didn't have time for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know anyone who attempted to go in?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us shift gears to some of the items that you had talked about briefly on direct examination, and I'd like to talk with you -- about in your 1999 statement about the dead bodies that you observed. And describing paragraph 58, and that would be paragraph 58 of 1177. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the first body that you talked about, that man as you note in your statement was in uniform. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, do you have any information with regard to his circumstances of death? Not how he died but the circumstances surrounding how he died.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: If you give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I think I said in there that they were both shot in the head. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that, sir. I'm asking you how he died. The circumstances of his death, whether or not it was during a combat, foray, or anything of those circumstances. You have you no knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you note in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There may be confusion. We're talking about dead bodies you observed described in paragraph 58. Mr. Kehoe, you were talking about a man in a uniform, which appears to refer to the first finding of a dead body of a male. And in the answer of the witness, he referred to, They were both, which seems to refer to the second incident where a male and a female were found dead, and that female -- that male was also in a uniform, so I'm confused about which event you are asking about and whether it's the same event as the witness is answer relates to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher, I'm going to ask you about both events. And let's talk about the first one, when you're talking about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I missed that when he talked about both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "I'm talking about the individual man camouflage that was shot in the head.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question remains the same. You don't know the circumstances as to how that person died?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now this event I trust was August the 8th, and I take that from the fact that you say the next day after, you had been out on the street on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I believe it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you note that in paragraph 58, that he had been dead for some time.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now even given that it's the summer and warm, you don't know whether or not that person was killed on August 4th, August 5th, or whenever, do you?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The same is true of the next two bodies, the male and the female. Now I understand that the female doesn't have a uniform on, but the male does. They likewise had been dead for some time, as you say in the statement. And you don't know the circumstances of that death either.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, Mr. Boucher, that during your travels around and everything that you talked about in your statement, other than that woman that you describe in paragraph 58, all of the male bodies that you picked up, all the bodies you picked up, had camouflage on, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I'll just correct you. We didn't pick up any bodies, but we came across and found. They were all in uniform except -- and I don't recall. There was a person in a car that it looked like a tank had rolled over, squished the car, and there was arm sticking out. I don't remember if the arm had a uniform on or not, and I didn't know if it was a man, woman, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
