utterances.text: Now, this male and this female, how far were these bodies from the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Complete opposite end of -- they were actually outside of the town of Knin. You go up the hill, going towards Zagreb or Gracac. And when you reached the complete top of the hill, that's where the little tractor and trailer and the two bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, let me turn our attention to a couple of other items quickly. And I -- in your first statement, we're shifting gears now, sir, and we're going to start talking about a couple of items that took place within the compound after the -- the displaced Serbs came in. I'm sure there were Croats too, but the people came in.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in paragraph 7 -- let me say initially, I mean, in paragraph 7, and this is, again, for the record, P1176, you note there was one report of a rape by the Croat army, but it was changed to "the lady asked to strip, and they took her nice clothing." Now, tell us a little bit about this sequence of events. What you were initially told that this woman was accusing soldiers in the Croatian army of, and after further analysis, what actually took place.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: The first complaint to the CIVPOL was that she had been raped, and this was actually fairly important because we had in the UN all kinds of comments to really document this closely, because it is a scenario that was used in other parts of the former Yugoslavia. And upon trying to question this woman more and more to get more detail, where, when, who, what, you know, anybody present, whatever, she recanted her story and said, Actually, they asked me to just take my clothes off, and they took my clothes. But we reported it anyway in case again she would recant her story to something else later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you conclude as a police officer that many of the stories or some of the stories that you were receiving from people coming in there were exaggerations, or didn't hold up under scrutiny, either one or the other?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It was very common to receive all kinds of different stories that you had to document and look deeper, because people would jump to conclusion. It became fear, I think, and propaganda. Once we tried to document facts, what exactly, who was there, and so on, and so on, a lot of it fell apart. Or, it's reported from another person, another person, and so on, that also, in most cases, fell apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Boucher, did it fall apart because at least to some degree that the interpreters were giving you information that they wanted you to hear?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: The interpreters were scared themselves. If you remember in my statement, most of the interpreters were -- were Serbs. There was only a few that were Croat. Some of them actually had to be enticed to come to the gate, We need your help when people are coming and speaking the language and asking things so that we can provide some kind of service. If it is open the gate to receive them as refugees and so on. And through their fear, I think there is a lot of different stories that came about, and we tried as best we can. Remember now, our CIVPOL number is quite a bit lower. We're trying to determine what exactly happened, and some of it was not -- was exaggerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the exaggerations that you heard in UN Sector South headquarters, you also heard the same from the military arm of things as well, didn't you? I'm talking about the UN forces that were there.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, to a concern degree, again, I saw through police eyes more than military eyes. One comment I made earlier is I don't think there was 10.000 soldiers out there, but this is what the word that was -- was put out as.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that was Colonel Leslie who told you that?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes. There was some bad, I think, publicity or media reports and conflict, I think, that happened before Storm, before the Storm between the Croat authorities and the media, including the media reporting through the UN --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You're talking about Mr. Roberts.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, yeah. I think he was part of this. But even, I think -- I think the Canadians probably since the Medak Pocket in 1993, there was some bad feelings in there. They saw themselves as - the military I'm talking about - as peace keepers, and all of a sudden, they were in combat. Because I heard comments about this from the other Canadians. Not being a soldier, you know, and trying to be impartial, remembering what my briefing was in Ottawa before I left, try to stay the middle of the road. You have to listen to both sides, and don't jump do conclusions, and so on. So my comments are put -- as much as I can in those context. And I'm not saying, by the way, that the Croats weren't -- they weren't helpful. The military was not helpful in giving us access that we needed to really monitor. There is some negative aspect to this. It would have been easier if we could have been able to really document right away and have clear access to wherever we wanted to go right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Boucher, Colonel Leslie told you about these 10.000 troops which you concluded was an exaggeration. I want you to listen to a tape from a radio broadcast in Canada from the 21st of July, 2003, in a show called "Sounds Like Canada," and this is General Leslie speaking. It has been received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can play this at minute 2:43 through 3:10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, have transcripts been provided to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the relevance of this transcript is to the answer of the witness. I don't think they're related.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the problem is I do not know what questions Mr. Kehoe will put to the witness after he has played this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's an audio, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's an audio. I take it that you have some relevant questions after we have listened to this audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Kehoe, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the technological issue is, Your Honour. We tested this before we came in to make sure it was working. I can just read the transcript and just go from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you can do that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please just let us know what segment are you going to be reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It would be page 2, and it would start from the last sentence of the third paragraph: Back then, in 1995 ... Do you see that? And then it moves done down to the next line: "I'm a gunner."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, and keep your speed of speech in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just allowing the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm just -- the experience is that when you start reading that it goes up quickly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "Back then in 1995 he was a colonel in a Krajina capital of Knin." This is Colonel Leslie. "I'm a gunner. I'm an artillery officer, a professional, a professional. So I can comment on it with some degree of validity. This was deliberate targeting on a massive scale of residential areas. Why? Because I believe it was targeted to break their well to resist. And by the way, it worked. It killed a lot of civilians, and we'll never know the exact number. But estimates -- estimates -- estimates range from 10 to 25.000 dead."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Boucher, you mentioned to us preliminarily that there were bad feelings by the Canadian military resulting from the Medak Pocket operation. Do you believe that the Canadian experience in Medak Pocket affected the objectivity of some of these Canadian officers and enlisted men when they were reporting as to what was happening in Knin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if a foundation could be laid as to the witness's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He has not asked for any knowledge. He is asked for his belief, as a matter of fact. Belief is usually not that relevant. And if we would like to know whether they were influenced, I think that would need a kind of expertise of which I have some doubts as whether this witness disposes of that. But if you want to explore that, and use your time for that, Mr. Kehoe, you're free to do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you answer that question, sir?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I believe it could have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No I asked -- I gave you an opportunity. I said you were asking for a belief, and we have heard the beginning of the answer, he could have had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Of course, but why could you exclude that it could have had. That's exactly the kind of asset, the balance to theories, thoughts, et cetera, and facts, that the balance should be more to the facts. I gave you then an opportunity to say that if you're asking for an opinion, then especially in relation to this question, then at least you should first explore on what basis, that is, on the basis of what expertise, this witness could draw such a conclusion. Because I'm afraid that if we would have a are professor in psychology before us, he might be hesitant to answer that question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher, did you have conversations with Colonel Leslie or General Forand or other members of the Canadian contingent in Knin about their experiences in the Medak Pocket?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I did not. My only recollection is there is an documentary film that plays on TV in Canada about the Canadian army confrontation at the Medak Pocket, and there's comment there, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Moving to -- back to the actual transcript, sir, without -- that I read to you which is D329, when you were there in Knin, was there -- and General Leslie says that the estimates range from 10 to 25.000 dead, when you were there, sir, and out in the community and talking to the people, did you ever hear any number of dead that remotely came close to that number as set forth by then Colonel Leslie?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boucher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could start further cross-examination, but that would be seven minutes only. We are scheduled to resume this afternoon at 3.00. Now, I have received time indications of two Defence teams, each 45 minutes or less, at least it was less than 45 minutes, and the same for the other Defence team which brings me down, within one and a half hours. If these estimates are still accurate, then I leave it to you, Ms. Higgins, whether you would to start now or whether we would use the first session, which takes one hour and a half or a little bit more to hear the evidence in cross-examination by the two Defence teams. And then after the break, give an opportunity for re-examination and questions put by the Bench. Would you like to start at this moment, or would we have a break until 3.00?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm entirely in Your Honours hands and the Benches hands. I'm very happy to start for the next five, six minutes. I have a rather short section that I can deal with now. My estimate is approximately 50 minutes, Your Honour, so perhaps best that I commence now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- then perhaps we start at this moment. Mr. Boucher, you will now cross-examined by Ms. Higgins. Ms. Higgins is counsel for Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Boucher.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I would like to start just by asking you a couple of questions about your role in UNCIVPOL and the reporting mechanism to the Croatian police. Now, as I understand from April 1995, you held the position in Sector South as Sector Chief for UNCIVPOL, correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And that, in fact, after Operation Storm, you left as best you can recall on the 22nd of August. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I don't recollect this clearly, because I can try -- and I don't remember the dates. But I did -- it was the end of our mission. I did go with the other two Canadians who was the Sector North commander or Sector Chief and Sector East to the coast with the approval -- because we were actually supposed to go on holidays at the beginning of -- of August. And we delayed this because this was coming. So there is some days that I was not in the sector and the Deputy Chief was actually acting as the Sector Chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Let me try and assist you, Mr. Boucher, by directing you -- there's no need to call this up, but just so you can have a look at it. And the first statement that you make at the very end, paragraph 11, you confirm then that you took leave on the 22nd of August. Would you consider that to be a reliable statement that you made in 1996, shortly after the events?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I would have to say yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, when you went to Croatia, it was your first UN mission. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you speak any of the Croatian language yourself?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: When I arrived there, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Okay. I note that you yourself have said - again, I can direct you, it's in your second statement, but can you take it from me - that you stated that you didn't know very much about the conflict or about the area before you left. Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That is fair. I only received information and briefing about what to expect, and, again, directions, Stay fair, listen to both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You have, we know, extensive policing experience. You've confirmed to this Court that have you no military experience. Is that right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Is it also right that the nature of the briefing that you received when you were in Canada was non-specific in terms of what you were to expect when you arrived in Croatia, in terms of -- let me try and precise my question. In fact, what I'm actually -- let me ask you this instead. Once you had got to Knin and after Operation Storm itself, did you receive any specific briefing as to the functioning of the civilian and/or military structure within that liberated territory?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Are you asking about any directions from the UN that, for example, who would be responsible; or are you asking me did -- was there comments on television and newspaper about who was appointed?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: We'll come on that if we may. What I'm interested in is whether this was any specific detailed information which you were given as to how the institutions would function after Operation Storm, and by institutions, I'm referring to the civilian structures and the military structures.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I did not get official.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to confirm for me, did you have interpreters who were assigned to work with UNCIVPOL members?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Before Storm, yes. After Storm a lot of them moved and never came back, so we were down to not too many interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And is it right that in your role, you were involved with Mr. Elleby in drafting and working out a strategy of joint work with the Croatian civilian police?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You knew Mr. Romanic as the chief of the police administration of Kotar Knin, correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And he was one of your main points of contact within the Croatian civilian police. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher, I'm going to come on to look at the document about the joint work after the break. So we'll come back to that at 3.00. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher, we'll have a lunch break, and we'll resume at 3.00. Mr. Usher, could you already escort Mr. Boucher out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 3.00 this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the late start, but we had quite few matters, with the recess coming, which are also to the benefit of the party in this case. Are you ready to continue, Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Boucher, we were going to discuss the strategy of joint work that I understand you were instrumental in putting together with Mr. Elleby, and I'd like P240 to be brought on to the screen so you can have a look at the document itself. While the document is coming up can I just let you know for the record that this document is dated to be effective from the 26th of August, 1995, and I know that's a period when -- by which time you had left Knin but I'd like to just ask you about the principles that are set out herein and ask you to confirm a few points, if I may. The first is this. If you look at point 2, you can see there there is reference to the establishment of regular meetings with the Knin police department commissioner, it says Mr. Zedo, but it is Mr. Cedo Romanic. That was one of your intentions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Well, after Storm it became -- it was in the sector per se because the UN was really the one that determined that there was a Zone of Separation. The partnership had to be enhanced I think with the local police, because before that, it was a matter of finding -- for example we would find bodies, evidence, whatever it may be. We were not police officers to investigate but to turn over the information. So this was in light of making better cooperation that once we find evidence, information, regular meetings to make sure that we would work cooperatively.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And part that cooperation that you had set up is also reflected in point 3 which refers to daily liaison with the police stations. If you can see that in the first two lines?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And point 5, we see there there's reference to monthly, on a monthly basis to have meetings with the commissioner of the Zadarska, Kninska police department, Mr. Marijan Bitanga in Zadar and there's reference to Mr. Dragan Matic concerning the Drnis police. Again part of the intention, to increase cooperation in your role to monitor effectively the Croatian police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: This was not all my work, if you want, because my intention before I left was to establish some relationship. These people for example were identified here as the chief of the administration and so on. That must have been brought forward by Mr. Elleby who replaced me after I left, also replaced me during my absence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And just to complete analysis of this document, at point 6 we see that any problems that there were on the lower levels were intended to be resolved by Mr. Franjo Djurica. Can you see that in point 6?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I see it but I don't know Mr. Franjo Djurica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Another working relationship that you had established aside from Mr. Romanic was with the Croatian police chief in Sibenik, a man you have already mentioned by the name of Mr. Grgurcin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: From the limited time that you were able to see what was happening in Knin, can you help this Trial Chamber with the resources that the local civilian Croatian police had to their access for them to be able to use, to your knowledge, the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I don't recall -- and I'm not sure what -- what type of resources you're talking about. Human resources or equipment?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: For example, human resources, vehicles that they could use, can you assist us with that?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I know before I left I had asked the CIVPOL monitors to work very cooperatively with the police to -- for more than one reason but one of the reasons was to establish a sense of normalcy for the community. There was more and more Croatian residents and maybe even of Serb ethnic origin coming back to the community to their houses and so on, people who had been away for four years, so to get things going really, really the authority for policing was the policija.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: The -- our authority was based on monitoring and monitoring human rights, monitoring several things. And of course if there would have been issues at that point with the minority Serbs that stayed behind, in fractions, so on, of course you can deal with it fairly quickly. That was my intention. But how it was pursued after I left, I have no idea how things turned out.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And presumably you have limited knowledge given the time that you were there in terms of the actual resources that the Croatian police had. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That is very fair. I would only add just a few things. One is the CIVPOL monitors were not armed and one of the policies we had, is we were not to pick up unless there was a serious injury somebody who was armed. So to have in our vehicle, for example, a policija, or have somebody who was carrying a weapon, a military, was against our policy. And, again, for the reason that the CIVPOL monitors and stations would also receive complaints sometimes so there was really two source. If somebody could approach the local policija and say there is an issue, there's an infraction, there's a crime, they could also do it through the medium of the CIVPOL police and it was important to keep the two avenues. Because they were afraid. They would never go to the policija until you establish credibility again. And so after I left, I don't know what exactly happened there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Just so that I understand the remit of your knowledge, Mr. Boucher, and your experience, can you please ask you to briefly have a look at P962.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If that could be brought onto the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The document that you're going to see is an organisational chart of the Ministry of Interior. And what I'd like to ask you is to just run your eyes across the names in that document. And I'd like to know whether or not you were familiar with the higher echelons of the Ministry of the Interior. If you look towards the bottom third, you'll see the name Cedo Romanic, and you will see the police stations underneath. Can you see those?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: You have to go a little bit further down.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see it now. Yes. There's also names further, higher, Marijan Bitanga, Ivica Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you meet either of these gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If you -- you have seen the top of the screen. Were you familiar with any other names within the Ministry of the Interior that are marked there?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I am not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Could I just ask you to confirm, Mr. Boucher, that the work that you undertook in your role with UNCIVPOL and your liaison with the Croatian police had nothing at all to do with Mr. Cermak, did it?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I think you're probably right on that point. The only -- the only time really where I met Mr. Cermak, I was under the authority of the commander. It was code red, and Mr. Cermak came to the UN camp --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Could I stop you there, Mr. Boucher, because I will come to that on a separate issue. So if I could ask to come back to that in a moment. Just to conclude the section on UNCIVPOL and the civilian police, can I ask you to clarify for me how it was that you and your associate members of UNCIVPOL reported the crimes that you came across to the Croatian police? How did that happen; how was it done?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: My direction was to all station commanders when we reopened the different stations or offices that if you come across a crime or report a crime, sometimes when you investigate, it becomes nothing, but report that as soon as you can to -- locally to the policija. In some cases they would not know it because nobody has reported it. That was the process. It also meant that we were to report what we found and also in what means who we contacted and to make sure there was documentation that certain things and complaints were actually passed on to the policija.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: From reading your statement, would it be right to say you make reference at one point about it being easier to talk to the police. Is it right to say there were oral reports to the police or were there also written reports, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: There was a lot more relationship with the policija before Storm and even after Storm, except for a few policija who obviously thought we had no business there anymore. But having said that, even before Storm, it was easier to organise a meeting to share what are the issues you have, because as I had said this morning, they were also informed through families and so on about things that happened in the sector, which they could not reach obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: So it was always very easy to deal in my mind much easier to deal with the policija than it was to deal with the milicija. And after Storm, at the beginning, let's say for several days after Storm the policija seemed like it didn't really have an engagement yet. The military was not out of the way to really -- to allow them to do as much. But as that grew, we asked them to get involved and we shared whatever we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And do you know whether, and if so how, that information was recorded by the Croatian police? Is that something within your knowledge or not?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It is not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It's right, I think, to say, again having looked at your statements that you yourself raised the issue of arson and looting with the police chief in Drnis, Mr. Bilac, and with Mr. Romanic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You were aware, again I understand the limited time you were there, and please correct me if I'm wrong but is it right to say that you were aware as would have been the normal course of events that the power to investigate those crimes lay with the Croatian civilian police. Is that -- was that your understanding at the time?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: If I go back to a statement I received from Mr. Grgurcin in Sibenik and my comment to him is, It's very difficult -- we don't have freedom of movement like we should have. And his comment is, The military is the military. They do what they want. And I also understood from that statement that if it's a matter of time until we can pull back and we -- or I should say the policija has a bigger role to play. But it's -- it's very fair to say also that when there's a military operation going on, the police, civilian police, takes a second stage. Not only for here. It happened in Quebec, in Canada. When there are certain situations and the military is called in to play a role, they take the first stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Boucher. The question I was aiming to ask was really to do with the reason you were reporting it to the Croatian civilian police was that you would expect them to be investigating the crimes that took place. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: More than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: My intention was to -- they knew or certainly ought to know who the different commanders of the military people that were involved, as an example the ones that I saw with the gas, jerrycans to at least get on them that this has to stop. And so more in a communication process and hopefully that would have been enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: From the observations that you made, it's right to say that it was your own observation that at the early stages the Croatian police were not, to use your words, really on top things. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That was my -- that's what I observed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In terms of your freedom of movement around the area, was it your understanding and your knowledge that Mr. Cermak had tried to assist on paper with facilitating a freedom of movement. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's the letter I received.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in practice, in terms you getting around the territory, after the first few days, let's leave that to one side, from reading your statement - and again if you'd like to look at, it's your second statement that you gave, paragraph 31 - you explain, and that for the record is P1177. No need to call it up unless it would assist the Bench. You explain in some detail that given your experience as a police officer, when you were stopped at the check-points you managed to the negotiate your way through and come to an arrangement to get you where you wanted to go. Is that a fair enough summary of how you managed to see what you needed to see, Mr. Boucher?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: This was done on a quite regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: The issue was more about the cemetery, that was the one area that was -- for some reason, couldn't get access for quite a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'll come on to that.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And it's right, again from your statement, paragraph 34 of your third statement, for the record P1178, that in seeking greater freedom of movement, in your position, you asked Mr. Grgurcin for assistance. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And in fact he told you to go to Cedo Romanic and you were given a paper that sometimes assisted, sometimes not so much. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now in relation to the Knin cemetery I would like to deal with that briefly. Again, I understand that you don't have military experience.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You firstly addressed, as you have been shown, Mr. Cermak, with your concerns about getting access. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: That was dated the 11th of August, which we have seen from the record. You can take that from me.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: For the record 65 ter -- sorry P1180, no need to call that document. On the 13th of August you were shown by my learned friend P1181 which was the response from Mr. Cermak informing you that he had passed on your letter to Mr. Romanic, and it would be he who would resolve the issue for you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive that letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in relation to those who turned you away, are you able to tell me or not whether they were military or civil protection units? Do you know, first of all, what the civilian protection units were?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So from that I can take it, can I, that you are not able to assist me with distinguishing whether in fact those people who turned you away were members of the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: The first time I tried to go there myself --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: -- with another monitor, it was military, other words, green uniform. And after this, it was policija. The best I can recall, it was blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: We know from a document that is already in evidence in this case, for the Bench's record P33, it's a HRAT report, Mr. Boucher, dated the 15th August that although a team had been turned away at some point, on the 15th, access was granted an hour and a half later that same day. Were you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware that the civil protection units were in fact part of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Were you aware of the role that they had, in terms of security of establishments such as the Knin graveyard? Was that in your knowledge or not?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move now to deal with the matter that you have raised concerning the meeting or at least when you saw live - again to use your word, Mr. Cermak - and that was in the UN camp. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Was that the only time you saw him, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's the part that is a bit foggy because I think it was actually twice. So I'm not positive. Once for sure, because I remember that one time where when he came in to -- right inside the gate of the UN camp and there was also a cameraman like the media was along. But I think there was even a second meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Let's take it in stages. Were you present on the 7th when we know that Mr. Akashi visited the UN camp.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you per chance see Mr. Cermak then, who we know visited the camp on that day? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It is very possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now the occasion that you talk about in your statements concerning Mr. Cermak being at the camp, did you come to know that on the 7th of August General Forand had met with General Cermak and that it was during a meeting on that day that General Cermak asked for access to the -- to meet with the displaced persons in the camp. Is that within your knowledge, Mr. Boucher?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That part, no; but I do have knowledge that there was several requests to see the list of all the refugees that came in to camp by different people. And again I don't recall today if Mr. Cermak was one of them but Mr. -- or the Colonel Zelic on several occasion even had a meeting. I remember escorting him from the gate to the headquarters where General Forand was, and there was other people. When I visited Cedo Romanic at the policija office also requesting the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Let me try and assist you, if I can, by refreshing your memory. In your second statement, paragraph 63, you will see, if you take a look, that you explained that you came to know that General Cermak requested through the liaison officer that he wanted to meet all the refugees. That was certainly within your knowledge, Mr. Boucher, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That part was, yes. Because I was requested to see if there was a committee, if a committee to be identified to represent the refugees, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And if I can try and assist you further, I'd like us to look at a record from the time, because it is a matter of evidence before this Court that is undisputed that the meeting that you're talking about where Mr. Cermak comes to the camp is on the 8th of August. So just to give you the opportunity to look at a contemporaneous document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If I could have P29, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: While it's coming up, Mr. Boucher, just to explain its context to you, this is a report that was made issued -- daily report issued by the HRAT team, the name of which you may be familiar, the Human Rights Action Team in Knin. And if you could look at the very bottom of that page, this is reference there -- sorry. Could I ask you in fact --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Could I have the second page of that document, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If you look at the bottom two lines you'll see reference there to: "Today, however, General Cermak came to the compound and in the UN's presence delivered to a committee of the DPs," over the page please, "the Croatian government's position regarding their reintegration." That paragraph there at the top of the page, I won't read it out in full, but if you just take a moment to scan it, Mr. Boucher, it refers to Mr. Cermak announcing to the displaced persons the range of rights that would be guaranteed for them. Is the record there, does that accord with your recollection of what Mr. Cermak had to say that day?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you have any further recollection about the way in which Mr. Cermak addressed this issue with the displaced persons and the committee?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I don't, because the decisions were from the commander, not from me. So I was an observer and limited, at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: One point that you have made clear to us in evidence before this Court is Mr. Cermak wanting the people to stay in Knin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And you'll see reference there again in that paragraph that I just referred to as Mr. Cermak not wanting a dead town. Can you see that on the fourth line from the bottom of the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I -- I don't recall that comment, to see a dead town, but I remember the fact that whoever wants to stay can stay. This may have been an issue of interpretation, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you come to know about the provision of assistance to those people in the camp of blankets, food and cigarettes? Did you come to know about that?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I don't recall this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: And my explanation would be that when the refugees came in, we really had nothing, not even enough food. It became my responsibility with the CIVPOL monitors under the command of General Forand to please look after the refugees the best we could and at the same time also manning the gate, so looking after the refugees and also trying to provide enough food, which was short. We didn't have enough food, and there was even water issues for a thousand people plus all the UN, but the goal was to create a committee for them. They were there. If they could cook themselves, if we could try to supply -- it started out with eggs and, you know, minimal, cheese and whatever we could gather, to cook, clean and so on and really look after themself and identify to some of the CIVPOL monitors if they needed, for example, medical assistance and whatever. So once that was created as a committee, I was a bit away from it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: So you're not sure how that matter was resolved in the end --

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- effectively? Did you come to see a follow-up letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If I can ask for P388, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: A follow-up letter sent by Mr. Cermak to General Forand straight after that meeting on the 8th of August?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I will try to inject more pauses.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If I could ask to you just peruse that document.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I do not remember seeing this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You can see there, perhaps, however, having been at the meeting, that there's again reference to trying to assist with the conditions of normal life for the displaced persons in the camp. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'd like now to deal with a new topic with you, Mr. Boucher, which concerns the title and appointment of Mr. Cermak. And I'd like to deal firstly with the fact of his appointment, if I may. I know from the first statement that you made back in 1996 - and again, you can take it from me, if you'd like to check, it's paragraph 8 - and the wording ask as follows. You say: "General Cermak was appointed by Mr. Tudjman on approximately the 6th of August, 1995 to be the governor of the Knin area." Now either at any time during your stay in Knin or thereafter, did you come to know that he was in fact appointed a day earlier, on the 5th, and you're right to say by President Tudjman. Did you know about the date of the appointment being the 5th?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In your second statement that you made, for the reference it's paragraph 62, and again if I could just read the piece to you so that you're following with me, you state that: "About three days after the attack, I watched local Croatian TV where President Tudjman announced that he had appointed General Cermak as governor of Knin. I had never heard of General Cermak prior to this." Do you remember where you were when you heard this broadcast?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I believe it was a TV that was set up in the UN camp to monitor, you know, what was presented on different channels. And again there may have been a delay with the media, you know, finally announcing this. But it could have been 7th, could have been 6th. My comment about I didn't know about this, this was also reported by interpreters --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: -- that he had been appointed so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I was going to come on to ask you that, how it was that you came to understand that was being said.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your understanding was through an interpreter. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Several of them. Through the media relation office also the UN. At the UN camp there was an office that dealt with media.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You've mentioned that and you have dealt with that in the statement that you recently gave to the Gotovina team. Just to touch upon Mr. Cermak himself so that I'm clear about your testimony, it's right to say that you never had a one-on-one meeting with Mr. Cermak. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Is it also accurate to say - and again to be fair to you - that you didn't have any personal firsthand knowledge of what his actual role was?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes. At any stage again either during your stay in Knin or thereafter, did you come to know about Mr. Cermak being tasked with being a point of contact for the UN?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did you come to know that part of his role concerned normalization of life in Knin and assisting with this issue of the displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Again, I didn't know that. If I can just repeat what I said earlier. A lot of this information would have been shared with the commander, General Forand, because this was all under code red.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: So I was not in authority to make any deals or agreements.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I understand. I'm actually just going to give you an opportunity to deal with it because I'm going to come on to a point that may be more difficult in a moment. Again, for the sake of clarity, right that you yourself never went to his office in Knin. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And it would be fair to say that you were never told or informed yourself about the level of staffing he had in the garrison?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Or the resources that he had available to him. Would that be true?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, in the first statement that you gave, as well as providing information about Mr. Cermak's appointment, you also explain a little from your understanding as to who was in command of the army and the police, to remind you, paragraph 8 of the first statement, we're introduced to the gentleman named Colonel Zelic and you say: "The Croat military was under command of a Colonel Zelic." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: True. That's the first contact I had with anybody from the Croat army, who showed up with some authority and wanting to -- well, again wanting to have the list of refugees but saying that he was speaking on behalf of the Croat army.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And in fact you give us more detail in your second statement when you explain that he came to the camp on, you believe, the 6th of August. And he introduced himself as the commander of the army. Correct? You can have a look at paragraph 53, if that helps, of your second statement, Mr. Boucher.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's what I wrote so I would think that's the information I received through the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And that you in fact dealt with him in trying to assist yourselves getting access out of the UN camp?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: In terms of the police in your first statement you refer us to, of course, Cedo Romanic who was, you say the new chief of police in Knin. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And you refer to us Goran, Goran --

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Grgurcin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Exactly. Thank you. I have been doing so well with that name up to now. In terms of his position as the chief of police for the Drnis area out of Sibenik. Do you recall that from your statement?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: One observation that you provide for us, in terms of General Cermak, can be found at paragraph 65 of your second statement, and again I'll read it out for you, Mr. Boucher. "General Cermak did not appear to me to be a military man. He did not carry himself in that way. He did not have an aura of authority. His hair was long. I think he wore a uniform. This was the only time I saw General Cermak live. However, I saw him several times on TV." Is that an accurate and fair summary today of your impression of Mr. Cermak, from when you wrote that statement?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I would agree with this. But you know today the more I try to remember, I don't even think he was in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to now give you the chance to examine with me finally before I close the third statement that you made. For the record, it's P1178. If you have that before you, Mr. Boucher, we know from the front sheet of that interview that you were interviewed on the 3rd and the 9th of April, and you signed the document on the 5th of November, 2008, a short time ago. Do you recall giving that interview?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Present during that interview the names are cited on the front sheet. They are Ruth Frolich, Brian Foster, Katrina Gustafson and Deon Van Rooyen. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Did those interviews take place in The Hague or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: This was telephone interviews.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know -- well, for starters, did you yourself either record the interview or did you take any notes during the interview?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I did take a few notes but a lot of it was referring to the previous two statements I had submitted, and what it was is, they did the transcribing, send it back to my assistant so that I would proofread it to make sure and I made the corrections that I thought should be made and then forwarded back the -- a copy and upon my arrival here gave them the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Were you ever provided with a tape-recording of the interview that took place?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Do you still have the notes that you made during that interview? I know it's probably difficult for you to recall.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I don't think I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Now, during the telephone interviews that took place, first of all, how was it that you came to sign the document? Was it faxed over to you and you faxed it back?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It was actually -- I don't think it was through fax but through e-mail. And it was sent back without the signature, until all the corrections were made. At that point once it was correct, I signed it and then we e-mailed it back. And the message attached to this was, Could you please bring the original when you arrive here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Sure. Thank you. During the telephone interviews that took place, were you yourself given any further information about Mr. Cermak by any -- anybody who spoke to you on the phone?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I'm not sure what information you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm just asking whether in fact you were given any information as to what Mr. Cermak's role was or who he was. Was there any information that was passed your way that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like you to now just have a look, please, at paragraph 43 of your third statement. I'll read the extract into the record. It's a short extract. "As governor of Knin, I believed Cermak was in charge of both the military and the civilian authority in Knin. I base this on the fact that it was announced on TV that he had been appointed as some kind of governor of Knin. Interpreters and civilians I spoke to told me that this meant that he was the military and civilian boss of the area." Dealing with the title first, and I see clearly there that have you inserted the word "believed." I want to deal firstly with the title. Did you come to know at any point that he was not in fact the governor of Knin but was appointed as the garrison commander of Knin?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear that title.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you for the record, and for your benefit so you understand my questions, a contemporaneous document which is D31, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: If that can be brought up onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: As it's coming on to the screen, to put it into context it's a document that this Chamber is extremely familiar with, and I hope they will indulge me by presenting it to you, Mr. Boucher. It's a document dated 5th of August, 1995, and as can you see from its content, it's a decision issued by Franjo Tudjman appointing Colonel General Cermak as the commander of the Knin garrison. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I know you had a media department, as you have explained to us. I'd like to finally give you the opportunity of looking at D36, please, which again refers to the same point. Is it right that you had people reviewing the media articles that were coming in so that you could appraise yourself of what was happening in the area? Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: We did have a media -- the information wasn't always fanned out, though, to everyone particularly at that hectic time. We were -- we had our hands full.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I can imagine. I understand. If you can take a look at this article and tell whether or not you ever saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: For the record, it's a press article which was published in Slobodna Dalmatia dated the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And in that first paragraph you see reference again to the decision appointing Ivan Cermak as the commander of the Knin garrison. I understand and I think it's right to say that the information you got, you relied on interpreters to give it to you. Correct.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: You also fairly state in that paragraph 43 that we've just looked at, that it was your belief that he was in charge of the military and civilian authority, and that you based that on the announcement on TV, and that the interpreters you spoke to gave you the information that he was the military and civilian boss. That was the sole basis, wasn't it, Mr. Boucher?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And just to clarify, did you ever come to know that in fact Croatia didn't have in fact the position of a military governor? Was that something you came to know or not?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: When the interpreters said that to me, one of the interpreters, the first time, I thought governor? What does that mean? And apparently comments were that person is responsible for the Knin area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: To put this -- yes. But you didn't in fact know what he was responsible for, did you?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I was -- I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: And it's right to say that you never saw any orders that were issued by Mr. Cermak to either the military or the police. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I never saw any orders, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you provide me with any of the names of the interpreters or civilians that you spoke to about this?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: You know, most of the interpreters it was by first name, Tanja or -- there was a young woman by the name of Lily but family name, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher, thank you very much for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Higgins. Your estimate of time, Mr. Kuzmanovic, is still the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will done by the balance of the day. Just joking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You know my sense of humour, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I should be no more than 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed. You will now -- Mr. Boucher you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kuzmanovic, who is counsel for Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher, I'd like to take you to your statement, P1178, please. Paragraph 38. And please let me know when you get there.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Could you tell me which statement this is. They don't have numbers on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. It's the one dated 11/12 November 1999. I'm sorry, it is not that one. It is 3rd and 9 November 2008 and 5 November 2008.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: And which paragraph again, please?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: There's a gentleman there in that paragraph identified as Nelson Garcia. Is Nelson Garcia, was he an intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: To my knowledge he was not. He worked under the UNCIVPOL headquarters in Zagreb. He worked under relationship with the policija out of Zagreb, but not as intelligence. It was more operational in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of contact did you have with Mr. Garcia subsequent to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: May have been with telephone conversation. I don't even know if there was communication, written communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I think you said you were being based in Knin, that you weren't necessarily aware of the structure of the Croatian Ministry of Interior and how the police was structured after Operation Storm. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Garcia was aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I would think he would be, because it was more at his level from the UNCIVPOL headquarters to the head of the policija in Zagreb. So I would think, it's a guess, but I would think he would be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher, this is not a criticism of you at all, but would you agree with me that had Mr. Boucher -- or had Mr. Garcia been aware of how the police was structured that it would have been beneficial to you in your work in Knin to know the various structures were involved after Sector South became liberated?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: It certainly would have been beneficial, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you, please, D497.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the ... the attachment on there, Mr. Registrar? Is there no attachment to that? Is it ... That's not the document. I must have it written down incorrectly. I will move on and I'll come back to this. One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: My question I guess, before I get back to this other document is: You work with Mr. Elleby. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So you were basically the person in charge up until the time you left in roughly August 22nd or so?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Elleby was your number two?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Who, if you could tell me, what other people did you have with you in your office that you worked with on a daily basis from UNCIVPOL? If you could give me some names.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: You're talking about at the Knin level?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: There was one police officer from Lisbon, Gustavo was his name, I forget his family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you work with a Mr. Romassev?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That name's familiar and I believe he was working out of the Knin station, not the Knin headquarters of CIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Describe the difference between the Knin station and the Knin headquarters of CIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: The directions for the UNCIVPOL was given to the Sector Chief, the Deputy Chief and administrative officer and humanitarian office and some support in translations and maybe secretarial. The rest of the UNCIVPOL officers were actually working in offices in detachments or stations. Knin was one of them. So if people were to approach with a complaint, they would go to the station, not necessarily to the Sector Chief or Deputy chief, if you understand. So policies and directions for UNCIVPOL at the sector level was the responsibility of the UNCIVPOL headquarters and that would have been myself, the Deputy Chief, the admin officer, and the humanitarian officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So if there was a complaint, for example, somebody wanted to report that there was a dead body or that perhaps there was evidence that a crime had been committed, they wouldn't come to you; they would come to the office. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Generally that would be case unless they knew me or they saw me somewhere, and what I would do is I would probably relay the message to one of the UNCIVPOL monitors to please go to that location and have a look and make the local contact with the policija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, would they issue a daily report to your office?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: They would. Every station would have their own report, what the monitors do and have to report every day. It was submitted to the -- the Sector South headquarters for UNCIVPOL. It was coordinated through an operations officer which was like somebody who answered the phone or relayed messages and so on. And that -- the station's report was actually put into an a sector situational report forwarded to Zagreb every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you would have several levels of reporting and as far as you were concerned, were you sort of the compiler of the reports that sent them along?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I would see the report every day unless if I was out of the office the Deputy Chief would either sign it, but I would usually see it when I came back. Like if I went to Korenica, for example, if I came back late that night or in the morning, I would definitely -- unless it was something out of the ordinary. But I would see this report. If I'm there on the spot, most of the time I would be, I would sign the report and send it forward to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's true, Mr. Boucher, is it not, that the information that you sent along, you yourself did not independently verify or confirm; it would just be information that you had received and then had passed along in another report to Zagreb, generally?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I would agree with you that most of the reports I would not have been on the scene. I would not second-guess or verify everything. Except if I was at the scene or -- then that way I with a know for sure. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it a general practice or a rule for UNCIVPOL members not to, for example, when they came upon a crime scene to disturb anything at the crime scene or to alter the crime scene in any way?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: My response may not be politically correct, but the unfortunate thing about the UNCIVPOL police monitors from different countries, some of them, and that's from their own comments, some police officers were in the mission and their comment was, Back home I'm only a police driver, or I'm only in charge of the police stores for uniforms or equipment or I'm an administrator, so the quality of investigation from one officer to another could have been good span, so -- during Storm and right after, there was a limited number of people so we tried to use everybody we could, so -- but, yeah, the reporting on some of them the English was very limited, coming from some countries just barely, you know if you see a report, then you probably have some of them are hard to decipher what exactly do they mean by this. So that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I guess the short answer to my question was you are not necessarily sure whether it was the general practice for UNCIVPOL members not to for example when the came up on a crime scene disturb anything at the crime?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I'm pretty that there are situation where they could have been disturbed because of a lack of police investigative experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I found the document, and of course I was incorrect. It was P497, not D497.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could pull that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher, this document is a document dated the 3rd of August of 1995. At that time, you were in Knin. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is pre-Operation Storm. And if you will take a look at the cover page, this document is addressed to the police administrations of various places, including for example Zadar-Knin and the second area being Sibenik which is where you had a colleague. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Sibenik police administration did not cover Zadar-Knin?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: You might be right, because I think they covered Drnis and -- part of it. The Zadar-Knin was out of Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you didn't have for example a chart or a scheme that showed for example if a crime occurred in Drnis, it would be reported to Sibenik or if a crime occurred in some other place, it would be reported to Zadar?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: No. If the crime happened in Drnis it would be reported at the policija office in Drnis, not in Sibenik. If it happened let's say in Gracac, it wouldn't be reported in Zadar. It would be reported at the policija office in Gracac. More local area, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This order and if you -- we will go to the second page, please. The second page notes that the order requires immediate setting up of police administrations in various areas obviously in preparation for what would happen in the event that the territory was liberated after Operation Storm. Were you given any information at all by your people in Zagreb that this was going to occur?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The next document I'd like to call up is 3D01-0076.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher, this is a document dated August 17th. You were still in Knin at that time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is a letter directed to the chief of the military police administration from a Mr. Moric from the Ministry of Interior of Croatia describing the situation involving burning houses, among other things and identifying that the perpetrators of the acts in most cases persons dressed in Croatian army military uniforms. Was that your awareness that the perpetrators of acts that you observed were dressed in Croatian army military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, there were also people who weren't members of the Croatian army who abused those uniforms that you saw. Is that not true?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D1219, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1219 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, please call up D499.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This document is dated also August 17th from Mr. Moric. And you had discussed issues regarding restrictions of movement during your examination. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is an order on the second page signed by Mr. Moric in the second paragraph asking in the police administration areas not to restrict the movement of people associated with the European Union monitors, UNCIVPOL members or UNCRO members. Were you aware of this order?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I notice on the order that it's top secret and it's also dated the 17th of August. My efforts to get more movement was way before that. But I never did see this report, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't necessarily ask you if you saw the order itself but were you made aware of it?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You had earlier discussed, Mr. Boucher, the issue of the churches and the fact that they were standing particularly Serbian Orthodox churches, whereas the Catholic churches that you'd run across, many of them had not been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to call up 44 -- 65 ter 4429, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document dated August 21st, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's an order again from Mr. Moric from the Ministry of Interior seeking information regarding churches and monasteries in the Orthodox diocese in the area asking for a report about what had been done to protect them and for a separate report regarding Catholic churches. Were you ever made aware of that report or did you ever have an ability to review that report?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I never saw the report. I was never made aware of this report, and if I look at the date, it's getting to the end of my stay in Knin. So maybe that information was passed on to my successor. I'm not sure, but I was never made aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1220, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Boucher --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, Your Honour.
