utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1220 is admitted into evidence. The reason why I was slower than usual, Mr. Kuzmanovic, is that the language in the previous document sounded so familiar to me that I wondered whether it would not be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You're referring to D499, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last one, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The new exhibit, the 65 ter that has just been turned into an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will check that. That was the letter from Mr. Moric about --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, that was the one before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is similar. It is different. There are two separate documents, Your Honour, relating to that. You are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll find the reference to the other document, Your Honour. I'll get it to the -- to the Chamber. Because it is similar to another document that has been previously marked and identified as an exhibit but it's not the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that would then be just for ... would that be D48 then, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you say it's different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because the language appears to be the same more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I looked at them both and I don't know if they're i-- the one that I have is different from D48. And if they're the same, Your Honour, I'll double-check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you'd please double-check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The last area, Mr. Boucher, is regarding UNCIVPOL itself. You said that you had over 200 members of UNCIVPOL in Sector South before Operation Storm, roughly before Operation Storm began. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I wouldn't say over. It was close to 200 but I think it was a little bit below 200, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the reasoning behind limiting the number of UNCIVPOL members after Operation Storm to about you said about two dozen?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: That was because we knew that the talks between the president was going nowheres. President Tudjman, Milosevic, we also knew that the Croatian army was getting very close, so I would -- I would say that the information we had within the UN ranks was there is a potential conflict -- not a conflict but a re-taking of territory and if you remember, of course on May 1st, Sector West went -- was -- went out. So I think the sheer deductions by most people involved was limit the number of people have you in sectors to -- to, you know, protect them if you want. And that was the discussion I personally had with the commissioner of the UNCIVPOL in Zagreb and my recommendation was when they end their mission because there is somebody leaving almost every month, please don't send a replacement until this clears up. And that's what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you think in hindsight it would have been better to have those 200 people in Sector South after Operation Storm under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: The reality is there was a lot of new monitors but without UN experience, a lot of them in Zagreb, ready to be deployed. But they were holding them in Zagreb until, you know, the final outcome, I guess. And after -- after Storm, I don't know really what happened, if we got any more help, because my tenure there wasn't very long. I had to go. End of mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: One other follow-up question in terms of the vehicles you had at your disposal for patrolling, Mr. Boucher. I think we had heard some testimony before that UNCIVPOL had two or three vehicles that they had to use for their patrol out of Knin. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact number but we had issues because we had a lot of vehicles hijacked by the Serb -- in the sector. We had lost vehicles. And every time monitors went to Zagreb, the vehicle didn't come back because nobody else came back to bring it back. So you're right. We were down to a few. The exact number, I'm not sure. I would estimate there would be more, because there was about two dozen. I would estimate there would probably be about seven or eight, in that neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's all the questions I have, Mr. Boucher. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been informed by my case manager that it is the same document as D48, only from a different source, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The handwriting on D48 misses at D1219 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but apart from that, it seems, as far as the content is concerned to be a similar document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We can withdraw that, Your Honour, if that is appropriate to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps D1219 could be vacated. Again it is not the same document but you refer to the content rather than to anything else and the numbers of the -- at the top are exactly the same, content is the same. Ms. Gustafson, before I give you an opportunity to re-examine the witness, if there is any need for that, I would like to invite the parties and I do it in the presence of you, Mr. Boucher, you gave an estimate of the distance from your house to the northern barracks as being approximately 500 feet, and you said not more than 600. Could I invite the parties -- we have map 29 in the binder which gives a scale and is not a distorted map. Looking at that map, I would come closer to 950 to a thousand feet than 600, which might be relevant; the difference between 180 metres and close to 300 metres might in relation to the matter concerned be relevant. Mr. Boucher, if have you any comment on what I just said, I looked at a map and thought that you might be a bit low in your estimate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I won't argue with you, Your Honour. You may have the best source. But I remember walking that distance often because at one point I was walking to the UN camp and within a few minutes I was at the milicija office or was close to the gate of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were apparently are in good shape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I invite the parties to agree on whether this -- whether there might be a bit of a low estimate -- assessment given by the witness. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just have one question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Boucher, a few moments ago you were asked questions about the possibility of crime scenes being disturbed by UNCIVPOL monitors, and I wanted to ask you more concretely, did you ever become aware of any specific situation where a crime scene was disturbed by an UNCIVPOL monitor?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no. But what I really was trying to raise is it was possible because we had -- all monitors had to have five year's police experience but it was a very diversified level of experience that they had.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question for you, Mr. Boucher. You described for the Chamber, if I could summarize it, the unruly behaviour of the soldiers, and you said this was different and you mentioned sergeants and higher-ranked military persons. Now, did you ever happen to see them together, that is, the sergeant and higher together with the soldiers, the ones behaving relatively well, and the other ones, the soldiers behaving unruly? And I'm asking you to in order to find out whether, if your answer would be in the affirmative, whether there was any initiative or response from the sergeant and higher-up level to those who behaved unruly.

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: The only time you could actually or at least I could see within the same view would have been right outside of the gate of the UN compound where there was, you know -- sorry, Croatian army vehicle parked there and a sergeant there which was actually a liaison. He stayed there a lot. He would only go away to get orders or directions and come back. Not far from him could have been, and there were sometimes, some private, I don't know if that is the right term, but lower soldiers. But -- and around him and whoever was running or controlling the tank, because there was a tank at one time right in front of our gate, like I said, a lot of the private would come right to the gate, point the gun it's just -- they were so excited to be there, asking the interpreters at the gate. So in the presence, yes. Were they in the organisational charts supervisors and so on? That, I don't know. I can't help you there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then my second question: Did they respond in any way to this unruly behaviour?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: I didn't observe that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, a similar question in relation to when you saw people taking out all kind of goods from the homes. Did you ever see higher ranking military persons nearby and -- or was it you just saw those privates, as you called them, doing these kind of things, in the absence of any higher ranking military men?

utterances.speaker: NORMAND JOSEPH BOUCHER
utterances.text: In my recollection, I've never seen rank beside them when -- what I consider things to be out of the ordinary. So it is basically at the lower level of the army. So -- and I think I mentioned that before, that it was a bit strange to see that but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Is there any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, Mr. Kuzmanovic, and Ms. Higgins, not. Then, Mr. Boucher, this concludes your evidence in this Court. I would like to thank you very much for having come a long way and I'm happy that we could conclude your evidence now so that there would be no need for you to return. I'd like to thank you for having answered the questions put to you by the parties and by the Bench. [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Merry Christmas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Boucher out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to deal with a few procedural matters. It will not take very long but if we would start with it now, we might not all be properly prepared, which could result in it taking even more time than necessary. I would like to go through the exhibit lists still outstanding. There were some objections I think it was in relation to Mr. Turkalj. I would like to deliver one or two decisions. I would like to give an opportunity, at least that was reported to me as the wish of the Gotovina Defence to address the matter of Rule 70 issues in relation to the New York Times article, to make a brief submission. Is that correct, Mr. Misetic? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like then to do that also after the break. Could you give us an estimate on how much time that would take? Because if it would be a long submission, I would invite to you do it in writing. If it would be a brief submission, I would give you an opportunity to do it now, after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to put it on the record, so it should take me less than three minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will have a break and we will resume although not for very long, I hope, at five minutes to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few housekeeping matters on my list. The first is the list of if I can call them Theunens's exhibits, on which no decision has been taken yet. Have you parties received a list, 18th of December, sent by Mr. Monkhouse to all the parties? It is a list consisting of 38 documents which mentions the 65 ter numbers, the provisionally assigned exhibit numbers, and the exhibit status, until now, and none of them being confidential. Are there any objections against admission of those exhibits? If you're not prepared for it, we'll, of course, wait for a moment. But -- a moment would then mean three weeks, but are there any objections against the exhibits which appear on the list as starting with P01182 up to and including P01219? Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We have no objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Cermak Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We have only one remark, not really objections and I think we solve it with Mr. Registrar. It is concern of 65 ter 1026 which was already tendered as exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That on my list has been removed already. So apparently you're then working from a list with 39 documents instead of 38. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber admits into evidence the documents for which provisionally were assigned exhibit numbers P01182 up to and including P01219. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The list will be filed so that we have a complete record of the 65 ter numbers to which these exhibit numbers were assigned. Then I move on to the list of exhibits in relation to the testimony of Mr. Turkalj. This list, sent to the parties, 18th December, contains 28 records, exhibit numbers provisionally assigned from P01220 up to and including P01247. Objections are there against P01221, P01222, and P01223, but from what I understand, these objections are mainly about the description, or am I mixing up now ... Yes, it's about comments in the relevance section of the application for admission; but it's not, from what I understand, objections against admission into evidence. Then I have another comment on 3508, 65 ter number, which is provisionally assigned P01226, and that was an observation in relation to what was a pending issue -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was an objection because P01226 was an exhibit consisting of an Official Note and the objection was raised, I think it was by the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Markac Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Markac Defence, yes. And the objection was raised also in view of the absence at that time of Chamber's decision regarding the admissibility of Official Notes of interviews. These were the Official Notes to which Mr. Zganjer testified. Now, the Chamber has meanwhile decided this issue. I don't know whether it was filed already or not. The Chamber has decided that the Official Notes are admitted into evidence with the exception of the Official Notes and one of them was already decided, Official Notes of the interviews with Mr. Markac and Mr. Cermak. One of them was already decided, so the decision for one of them gives just the reasons and for the other Official Note, it gives the reasons and the decision itself. Under those circumstances, where all the other Official Notes have been admitted into evidence, Mr. Mikulicic, would you first like to read our decision or could you already choose your position on the basis of this information? I leave it entirely --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would like to first read the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. Then the Chamber admits into evidence Exhibit numbers P01220 up to and including P01225. Then 65 ter 3508 provisionally assigned P01226 is marked for identification. The Chamber further admits into evidence P01227 up to and including P01247. Then I move to the last set, exhibits tendered during the testimony of Mr. Al-Alfi. I put on the record that there were objections against 65 ter numbers 4125, 4133, and 4252. Are there any other objections? These were the three documents which moved into an area which, for most of the documents, was not within the scope of the indictment. The Chamber has not yet deliberated on those objections. So 4125 is MFIed, 4133 is MFIed and also 4252 keeps the status of being marked for identification. Are there any other objections against the exhibits appearing on this list, the list in total consisting of nine documents? If not, then P01169 up to and including P01173 are admitted into evidence. Also admitted into evidence is P01175. All these lists will be filed so that they are on the record with all necessary details. Mr. Misetic, you asked three minutes to make further submissions on Rule 70 aspects of the New York Times newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I will quickly say this, and in addition, there's one other matter as to why the article is relevant. I wanted to put on the record that with respect to the Rule 70 issue concerning D1212 MFI earlier in this case a similar issue arose where internal Prosecution memoranda had been leaked to the press concerning my colleague Mr. Kehoe and on the basis of the press articles about leaked internal OTP memos a matter concerning Mr. Kehoe's eligibility was raised before the Chamber. The Gotovina raised at the time the issue of whether materials that would otherwise would be protected by Rule 70 could be leaked to the press and then those articles used in proceedings, and the Chamber in its 25 July 2007 order titled Order to the Prosecution concerning the alleged conflict of interest of attorney Gregory Kehoe at page 4 held that: "Rule 70 is concerned with restricting the Prosecution's disclosure obligations to the Defence pursuant to Rule 66 and Rule 67 and it is not relevant to the present matter." And the Chamber then proceeded to take into consideration the matters that were raised in the newspaper article containing information about internal OTP memoranda. The second -- a additional issue as to relevance that I'd like to raise is that this article is dated 21 March 1999 and exhibit P1144 which has been admitted into evidence is in fact a transcript of a conversation held between President Tudjman and General Cermak two days after that article was published. And if you look at P1144 at page 3, the president in talking to General Cermak says: "Who are those who gave testimony against you and the others, the thing that The Hague is now talking about? " That context of that conversation takes place as a result of the article that we have now tendered as MFI D1212. The transcript in 1999 was tendered by the Prosecution and therefore I would add that as an additional argument as to relevance, because it provides context as to why that conversation took place. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, any need to briefly respond to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I will try to be brief. Regarding the decision of the -- it was the Pre-Trial Chamber in July 2007 which was just Justice Moloto by himself I believe at that time, and that although the issue was framed as an issue of disclosure, it was in a very specific context which was when that was the only way to resolve the issue that was at stake which was -- I will stay vague because there were confidential filings, but about Mr. Kehoe's eligibility as counsel, and only by reviewing such material could the Pre-Trial Chamber reach the decision that it had to reach. But so first of all, the situation was completely different. And although framed as the disclosure, the reason that that material cannot be disclosed was because it is confidential and not to be used at trial. The Pre-Trial Chamber Judge Moloto, at the time the Pre-Trial Judge, was very mindful of that when he ordered the Prosecution to provide other materials he only ordered the Prosecution to do so to the Pre-Trial Bench and only later on in order to allow Mr. Kehoe to respond was he allowed to -- did he ask us, the Prosecution, if we would agree to Mr. Kehoe and the Gotovina Defence being able to review it. So that's just the clarification that I would like to make and that was the issue on the July 2007 decision. With respect to the presidential transcript, my recollection of that presidential transcript, the context of it is a little different. I would have to look at it again but I don't think that it's exactly as Mr. Misetic characterized and in any event I don't think that it makes it automatically relevant and of such relevance and probative value that the Prosecution should lose the Rule 70 protection, absent a waiver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 30 seconds, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 30 seconds Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just to address Mr. Hedaraly's position, I'm not asking for the underlying memoranda that were in the article and so therefore the issue as it related to Mr. Kehoe and then producing the underlying memoranda is not at issue here. The issue is whether the Chamber could consider the matters in a newspaper article. It did. We're saying just because it may -- the underlying memos may still be protected by Rule 70 doesn't mean that the Chamber can't consider just the article on its face. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I don't think there's any need, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the Chamber will consider the matter and -- Then I'd like to issue an oral decision. Well, as a matter of fact, it's not a decision. It's the reasons for a decision already given by the Chamber. These are the Chamber's reasons for granting trial-related protective measures for Witness 84. On the 22 October 2008 the Prosecution filed a motion requesting that the Chamber order the trial-related protective measures of pseudonym and face and voice distortion for Witness 84. On the 22nd of October, 2008, the Cermak Defence filed its response, indicating that while it did not oppose the request for protective measures, it disagreed with the Prosecution's arguments in support of the motion. It further indicated that by reason of the witness's job and the subject-matter of his testimony, it would be more appropriate for the testimony to be in closed session. The following day, the Markac and Gotovina Defence filed their responses, both requesting the Chamber to deny the motion. On November 3rd, 2008, having observed the emotional condition of the witness in court, the Gotovina and Markac Defence withdrew their objection to the protective measures request. They further joined the observation of the Cermak Defence on the need to hear the testimony of the witness in closed session. These submissions of the Defence can be found at transcript pages 11068 and 11069. On the same day, the Chamber granted the motion and decided that it would hear the testimony of the witness in closed session. This decision can be found at transcript pages 11069 and 11070. The decision was rendered in private session and the public is hereby informed about it. The Chamber held, in its reasons for its first protective measures decision in this case, which can be found at transcript pages 2610 and 2611, that the party seeking protective measures for a witness must demonstrate an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family, should it become known that the witness has given evidence before the Tribunal. This standard can, for example, be satisfied by showing that a threat was made against the witness or the witness's family. The mere expression of fear by a person is insufficient to justify protective measures. Witness 84 is a Croatian Serb who lives with his family in Croatia. The Chamber found that the expected testimony of Witness 84 could antagonise certain persons in the place where he and his family live. For two years after Operation Storm, Witness 84 received threatening calls from unknown persons who asked him why he was still working and living in his home town. After the witness's retirement in 1997, the phone calls stopped. Witness 84 further informed the Chamber that he was told by a witness who had already testified under protective measures in closed session in this case that local journalists had been pestering him to talk about his testimony. An additional issue for Witness 84's concern for his safety and a matter that has caused him some anxiety is that he was interviewed by one of the Defence teams at a police station in the presence of a Croatian police official. Witness 84 stated that the rumour that he had been interviewed spread and that he had decided to minimise his trips into town out of fear to be recognised. He further stated that in his town there was a negative attitude against Serbs and that he had been harassed in the street. The Chamber additionally considered the fact that the Defence withdrew its objections to the Prosecution's request. For the aforementioned reasons, the Chamber found that the Prosecution had demonstrated an objectively grounded risk to the security of Witness 84 should it become known that he had given evidence before the Tribunal. The Chamber furthermore considered that, in light of the nature of the anticipated evidence of the witness, the only effective way to protect his identity was to hear his testimony in closed session. And this conclude the Chamber's reasons for its decision to grant protective measures for Witness 84. Are there any other procedural matters the parties would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had during the testimony of Mr. Theunens several bar table submissions. They were given marks for identification ranging from D1107 to D1199. All those matters have been agreed between the parties and submitted to the registrar of the court, and we await their admission into evidence with the Court's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me be very open to you, Mr. Kay. When preparing this, I asked the staff whether we had a full list at this moment. It was not available. That's the only reason why we have not dealt with it. There is no reason to believe that where the parties have worked this out, that there's any -- would be any major obstacle against admitting into evidence, but this Chamber always prefers not to deal with matters if they're not fully on top of it. That's the only reason why I have not dealt with it. If you would insist to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. I can say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- have a session tomorrow morning, then we'll deal with it, Mr. Kay. Otherwise, you will have to wait till after the winter recess. I don't think that it will a major obstacle for the parties not to know our final decision on the matter to proceed in preparing for the remainder of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I won't be sacrificing my popularity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do have outstanding the Boucher statement, which is D1217, which is MFIed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have reviewed the statement. There is no objection to it. I'd just -- if we could get some guidance from the Chamber as to the timing of the disclosure. As I mentioned, it was disclosed in the cross-examination material and it's our position if the Defence wants to tender a 92 ter statement that we should get advance notice and I know the statement was taken last night but it would have assisted our preparation to have it last night as opposed to after our examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This seems to a very general call to receive statements which are sought to be admitted under Rule 92 ter as early as possible. That, I would say, goes without saying. Let me just check for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is aware of many aspects of it. Mr. Boucher arrived in The Hague recently. Taking the 92 ter statement under the present circumstances and also looking at its content might not have bothered the Prosecution greatly. Of course, this is an issue that if 92 ter statements are presented after the examination-in-chief has been concluded and if it creates substantial new elements, then of course lengthy statements whether we could immediately continue or whether that would be unfair to the Prosecution is still to be considered, but I hear that in relation this statement there's no objection, although some concern is expressed about the late timing of the disclosure. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. We would like to avoid the situation in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I appreciate that and certainly it was a situation because of the timing of it. But if we're on the topic of late disclosures, and I know I speak on behalf of all the Defence, if the Prosecution could work a little harder to get us proofing notes before ofttimes 9.00, 9.30, 10.00 the night before a witness comes on, we'd appreciate that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I earlier and could I say spontaneously already mentioned the proofing notes and the time of disclosure. So, therefore, that is not overlooked by this Chamber. D1217 is admitted into evidence. Any other procedural matter which --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: One brief matter, Your Honour. For a while now we had -- the Prosecution had what was referred to as the Cermak bar table motion and in the meantime many of these documents have been admitted on behalf of the Cermak Defence. There are two documents that are outstanding on the Prosecution's list to which we were told there were no objections so we just have those admitted so we can finally close the chapter on that bar table. Those are 65 ter 3530 and 65 ter 2552.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I reiterate what I said before, if I'm not on top of what it is about, I'll first check and then consult with my colleagues before any decision is given. But thank you for the reminder, Mr. Hedaraly. Any other procedural matter at this moment? Then I have a brief matter which I wouldn't call procedural, although it has got to do something with procedure. The Chamber was informed about a wish expressed by Mr. Gotovina to return the good wishes for Christmas, which spontaneously were given by Mr. Boucher. Now, as the parties are aware of, the Chamber certainly does not encourage exchanges of a more personal kind, but Mr. Boucher started, he was the one who wished us a Merry Christmas, so therefore under those circumstance the Chamber would not deny anyone to return those wishes but would also give an opportunity to Mr. Cermak and Mr. Markac whether they wish in these extraordinary circumstances to join in the return of the wishes expressed by Mr. Boucher. Because it is so unusual you might have felt it would be inappropriate but under the present circumstances I give you an opportunity to join if you wish to, Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CERMAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we do join in these good wishes of General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MARKAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, indeed I would like to join General Gotovina's good wishes too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the good wishes put on the little piece of paper by Mr. Gotovina will be relayed to Mr. Boucher and -- through the Victims and Witness Section and the message will be added to that that Mr. Cermak and Mr. Markac are joining in these wishes. Since we are talking the best wishes for Christmas, the Chamber would like to present the best wishes for the Christmas Days and for the new year to everyone in this courtroom. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think on behalf of all the Defence and the Prosecution we extend the Chamber the same, I'm sure speaking on behalf of my colleagues across the well. We extend the same wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is case law that there is latitude to return Christmas wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's right, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, therefore it is accepted, with gratitude, by the Chamber. We adjourn for the year, and we'll resume on Monday, the 12th of January, quarter past 2.00, in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
